articles.body: Maersk has announced revised Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) for shipments from Asia to destinations in Southern and East Africa. The new rates will take effect in November 2026 and remain applicable until further notice. Far East Asia to South Africa and Mauritius The revised PSS will apply from 9 November 2026. For shipments originating in Vietnam, it will take effect on 10 November. The origin scope includes China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. Destination All 20-foot containers All 40-foot containers South Africa and Mauritius US$1,000 US$2,000 China and Hong Kong to East Africa Maersk will also increase the PSS from China and Hong Kong to Kenya and Dar es Salaam from 9 November 2026. Destination All 20-foot containers All 40-foot containers All 45-foot containers Kenya US$1,000 US$2,000 US$2,000 Dar es Salaam US$1,200 US$2,000 US$2,000 For non-SPOT bookings, Maersk will determine the applicable rate using the Price Calculation Date (PCD). For non-FMC shipments, the PCD is the scheduled departure date of the first water leg shown when the booking is confirmed. For FMC shipments, the PCD is the final container gate-in date. For SPOT bookings, the applicable rate will be based on the booking confirmation date or the first vessel’s estimated departure date at booking confirmation. The surcharge will be collected at origin unless customers select different payment terms. Other local and contingency charges may also apply.

It was reported in August that Asso.subsea was buying Viking Reach from Eidesvik Reach, in which Eidesvik holds a 50.1% ownership interest and Reach Subsea 49.9%, with plans on renaming it to Arete. The vessel was delivered to the Greek company yesterday, October 26. "Named after the revered Queen of the Phaeacians from Greek mythology, a figure synonymous with wisdom, noble leadership, and providing safe harbor, TSV Arete embodies our continued commitment to excellence and reliability in marine operations," Asso.subsea said on social media. With its high-capacity subsea equipment, 70-ton AHC crane, integrated work-class remotely operated vehicle (WROV) and survey spreads, shallow water capability and extensive deck area, Arete is described as “an extremely flexible asset” , equipped for multi-purpose roles in subsea cable protection, route preparation, post-lay burial, and the offshore wind market. The vessel, which will hoist the Greek flag, follows the newbuild orders of the TSVs Avra and Andromeda. articles.body: Americas Offshore Chouest Group acquires Canada’s Horizon Maritime Bojan Lepic October 27, 2026 0 35 1 minute read Horizon Maritime Horizon Maritime US offshore services giant Chouest Group has acquired Canadian marine and offshore services provider Horizon Maritime, expanding its presence across Canada’s east and west coasts and into the Arctic. The Louisiana-based group has partnered with Horizon Maritime’s founders to acquire the St. John’s-headquartered company from CFFI and its lender HPS. The transaction’s financial details were not disclosed. The acquisition combines Chouest’s global offshore support fleet, subsea services, shipbuilding, specialised engineering, and marine technology capabilities with Horizon’s operations in Canada’s offshore energy and harsh-environment markets. The companies said the combination would let Horizon expand across all three Canadian coastlines, giving customers access to a broader range of marine transportation, subsea, and offshore services. Horizon Maritime will retain its existing management and leadership structure, with Steve Widmeyer continuing as chief executive. Widmeyer and company co-founder Sean Leet will also join the board of directors. Founded in 2015, Horizon Maritime operates in offshore energy, Arctic logistics, and specialised marine services. Its fleet includes the anchor-handling tug supply vessel Horizon Arctic , the platform supply vessel Horizon Dragon , and the icebreaker Polar Prince , along with three smaller utility tugs designed for operations in icy waters. The company also operates a Canadian harbour towage joint venture with Dutch towage specialist Kotug, established in 2019. articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Greece call for safe shipping routes, closer energy ties
articles.summary: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis held talks in Riyadh, pledging to deepen cooperation on energy, investment and digital connectivity as the countries marked 100 years of diplomatic relations. The crown prince received Mitsotakis at Al-Yamamah Palace, where an...
articles.body: Saudi Arabia, Greece call for safe shipping routes, closer energy ties in Hellenic Shipping News 27/10/2026 Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis held talks in Riyadh, pledging to deepen cooperation on energy, investment and digital connectivity as the countries marked 100 years of diplomatic relations. The crown prince received Mitsotakis at Al-Yamamah Palace, where an official reception ceremony preceded the talks, the Saudi Press Agency reported. In a joint statement issued at the end of the visit, both sides stressed the need to protect international shipping routes and keep energy supplies flowing without interruption. They expressed concern about attacks on energy infrastructure and their effects on supplies and market stability. Greece praised Saudi efforts to stabilize global oil markets and maintain supplies through alternative export routes, including the East-West Pipeline. The discussions also focused on expanding economic ties. The countries said bilateral trade reached about $1.7 billion in 2025, up from 2021, and called for stronger investment ties in infrastructure, construction, energy, logistics and technology. The talks built on a strategic partnership council announced during the crown prince’s visit to Greece in July 2022. The council held its first meeting during Mitsotakis’ visit to Saudi Arabia in January 2025. Among their energy priorities, the two countries pledged to accelerate work on the planned Saudi-Greek electricity interconnection. The project aims to enable electricity exchanges, improve grid reliability and strengthen power links between Saudi Arabia and Europe through Greece. They also agreed to explore opportunities to export clean hydrogen from Saudi Arabia to Greece and other European Union markets, while expanding investment in conventional and renewable energy and petrochemicals. Beyond energy, the two sides welcomed progress on the EMC submarine cable project, designed to strengthen digital connectivity between East and West, and pledged to coordinate its completion according to the agreed timetable. Saudi Arabia encouraged Greek companies to establish regional headquarters in the Kingdom and pursue opportunities linked to major projects, including Riyadh Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup. Greece, in turn, invited Saudi investment in energy, transport, logistics, digital infrastructure and advanced technologies, highlighting its position as a gateway to European markets. The two countries also pledged closer defense and security cooperation, including efforts to combat crime, terrorism and terrorist financing. They called for greater exchanges of expertise and training, along with cybersecurity cooperation and information sharing. On climate policy, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement. They also supported cooperation on the circular carbon economy, an approach to managing carbon emissions. The statement outlined further areas for cooperation, including artificial intelligence, space technology, health, education, culture, tourism and sports. Earlier on Sunday, Mitsotakis was received by the deputy governor of the Riyadh region, Prince Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Abdulaziz. Source: Arab News 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Nuclear ships only pay off under the IMO’s net-zero rules, UCL study finds
articles.summary: Nuclear propulsion can compete in container shipping only if an effective global emissions policy is in place and reactor costs fall sharply, according to new research from the UCL Energy Institute’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group. It is one of the most detailed total cost-of-ownership assessments of nuclear...
articles.body: Nuclear ships only pay off under the IMO’s net-zero rules, UCL study finds in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 27/10/2026 Nuclear propulsion can compete in container shipping only if an effective global emissions policy is in place and reactor costs fall sharply, according to new research from the UCL Energy Institute’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group. It is one of the most detailed total cost-of-ownership assessments of nuclear merchant shipping to date. The report, Nuclear Reactors for Merchant Shipping: A Total Cost of Ownership Assessment of a Low-Carbon Pathway, compares a large container ship (14,500 to 19,999 TEU) with nuclear propulsion against conventional fuel oil and dual-fuel ammonia vessels. It uses a literature review, interviews with five UK-based experts in law, insurance, classification, technology development and industry representation, and a cost model run with and without the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF). Key findings ● Policy sets the business case. Without the NZF, no nuclear vessel is cheaper than a conventional ship, even at the lowest assumed reactor cost. Under the NZF, nuclear vessels earn income by selling surplus units to other ships, which closes the gap. ● Reactor cost decides the outcome. Published estimates range from about 2,600 to 12,400 USD per kWe, a spread of nearly five times. At the low end, which assumes series production and deep cost reductions, nuclear is the cheapest option from 2040. At the high end, which reflects first-of-a-kind reactors, it is not cheapest in any scenario. ● The window is narrow. Surplus unit income is largest when a vessel enters service and shrinks as the NZF’s fuel targets tighten. Nuclear’s best chance to break into the market is early, not late. ● Faster is not cheaper. At 25 knots, the vessel sails 32% more distance a year but needs more than three times the installed power, and costs rise. ● Non-technical barriers are as large as the technical ones. Existing nuclear liability conventions were designed for fixed, land-based reactors. Interviewees expect no global framework for the first vessels, and a mature insurance regime could take 15 to 20 years. “Nuclear can compete, but only with much cheaper reactors and a global emissions policy, and neither exists yet. How both develop over the coming years will decide whether nuclear has a place in shipping.” said Farah Bziker, Researcher, UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group. Three features of the NZF support nuclear as a maritime energy source: a stringent fuel-intensity limit or steep reduction rate to ensure long-term demand; a stable, high-integrity surplus-unit market with a firm price; and a strong, sustained reward for zero- and near-zero-emission technologies. Policy that is less ambitious or less supportive of these technologies than the NZF will reduce nuclear’s potential. “Nuclear is not a reason to weaken maritime climate policy. It is one of the technologies that depends on it. Anyone backing reactor programmes should want a stringent international GHG policy and credible global framework,” said Dr Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport, UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group. The authors caution that the results may understate the true cost of nuclear shipping. The model excludes nuclear-specific insurance, reactor maintenance and hull integration, and treats decommissioning as a rough estimate. Vessels with first-of-a-kind reactors are not competitive, and it remains open who would bear their cost. A favourable cost comparison is also not enough: the first vessels will need agreements between states on liability, insurance and regulation. takeaways: It is one of the most detailed total cost-of-ownership assessments of nuclear merchant shipping to date.
Key findings ● Policy sets the business case.
Without the NZF, no nuclear vessel is cheaper than a conventional ship, even at the lowest assumed reactor cost.

articles.body: Industry Leaders Launch World’s First Maritime-Specific Cyber Vulnerabilities Database in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 Cydome, ClassNK, Bureau Veritas, MTS-ISAC and Rakuten Maritime announced today a collaboration called the Blue Initiative to provide the first public database of cyber vulnerabilities focused only on IT and OT devices that are relevant to the maritime industry, available for free at blue-initiative.org. With the rising number of vulnerabilities discoveries (more than 350,000 published CVEs and 200 entries added each day), identifying and prioritizing which system patches and cyber risks are relevant to each organization has become an extremely complex endeavor. This new initiative is designed to help shipping companies more effectively address the cyber vulnerabilities affecting the specific systems and equipment they operate by highlighting maritime-related equipment, ability to focus on specific vendors, and proactively alerting users when relevant new vulnerabilities are announced. “Identifying which vulnerabilities actually matter to the systems maritime companies operate is a major challenge”, said Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon, “and our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities. This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before. “ The Blue Initiative is an open industry collaboration, freely accessible at blue-initiative.org. Relevant organizations in the maritime community are encouraged to join and help expand the database. Effective vulnerability management starts with knowing which issues matter to the systems you operate. By focusing on maritime IT and OT equipment and bringing the community together to validate the data, the Blue Initiative gives shipping companies a practical, trusted resource. ClassNK is proud to be a contributing partner,” said Naoki Saito, General Manager, Ship Management Systems Department at ClassNK Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life. Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories. Bureau Veritas sees real value in a shared, maritime-specific reference that owners, equipment manufacturers and class societies can all rely on. We are pleased to join the Blue Initiative as a contributing partner,” said Panagiotis Anastasiou , Cyber Technical & Market Leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore. Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, The Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap. Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative,” said Christy Coffey, VP Operations at MTS-ISAC. Cybersecurity must be managed across a vessel’s entire operational lifecycle, from design through operation. As a provider of maritime cybersecurity, compliance, and digital solutions, Rakuten Maritime knows that tracking equipment vulnerabilities is critical to keeping connected fleets secure. By turning complex threat intelligence into actionable protection, the Blue Initiative gives operators the trusted reference they need, and we are proud to be a contributing partner,” said Ryan Son, Managing Director of Rakuten Symphony Singapore & Korea and Head of Rakuten Maritime. Entries in the new Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) are reviewed by cyber researchers from Cydome and the contributing partners, who validate and refine them before going live. Select entries also receive more elaborate analyst notes, and users will be able to: Browse vulnerabilities and their details Filter vulnerability searches to the equipment or vendors relevant to them. Access expert insights on vulnerabilities and their impact (select vulnerabilities, with more insights constantly added every day). Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities. “In most cases, vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, in line with standard responsible disclosure processes,” said Ayalon. “But the Blue Initiative links this intelligence to the specific vendors and systems that maritime users operate, allowing them to move quickly to patch and mitigate. Source: Cydome 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Fuel Switch Snapshot: Gas rally lifts LNG and LBM above LSMGO for Otto MS in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 In Rotterdam, LNG burnt in Otto medium speed (Otto MS) engines has flipped from a $23/mt discount to LSMGO to a $44/mt premium over the past week. Liquid gases TTF has strengthened amid supply disruptions at Norway’s Troll and Asgard gas fields, forecasts of lower temperatures across Europe and renewed geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, according to the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC). “Colder weather, low stocks, unplanned outages in Norway are all adding upward pressure on prices, but the single most important driver is still geopolitics and the risk of renewed military tensions in the Middle East,” said International Energy Agency (IEA) gas analyst Greg Molnár. Singapore’s LNG prices have risen by $82-83/mt depending on engine type. JKM prices have risen amid supply risks linked to tensions in the Middle East and forecasts of colder-than-normal winter temperatures in Europe, according to JOGMEC. articles.body: LNG shipping stocks: Qatar goes shopping in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 The UP World LNG Shipping Index fell 3.43 points (1.53%) to close at 221.48, a more moderate retreat than the prior week, while the S&P 500 lost 0.47%. Unlike recent weeks, the internals were soft too: the median fell 1.79% and the weighted index (wUPI) dropped 3.27%, with breadth of 8:13. The dominant story was news flow rather than price: QatarEnergy signed major long-term US supply deals — up to 4 mtpa from Cheniere through 2054, plus advanced talks with Woodside (up to 3 mtpa) and Venture Global — to cover its war-induced liquefaction outages, and the first Qatari cargo since April headed via the Red Sea to Poland’s Świnoujście terminal. ALNG led the gainers (+12%), with Tsakos +4.5% and the oil & gas majors (Chevron +3.65%, BP +2.2%, Shell +1.43%) all at fresh yearly highs. The fallers were led by New Fortress Energy (−16%, new lows), COSCO (−8.37%) and Pan Ocean (−8%), with ADNOC −7.25% and Korea Line −6.8%. In the background, gas prices rose in both basins on colder weather and strong Chinese spot buying — Asian LNG to $30.50/MMBtu, Europe just over $29 — while spot tanker rates firmed on Pacific routes to $30,750 (Atlantic $21,750). UPI & SPX The UP World LNG Shipping Index, which tracks 21 listed LNG shipping companies, lost 3.43 points (1.53%) to close at 221.48 points, while the S&P 500 index lost 0.47%. The chart below illustrates the performance of both indices with weekly data. Week 43-2026: Chart of the UP World LNG Shipping Index with S&P 500 (Source: UP-Indices) Broader View The UPI continues to fall at a more moderate pace. The median fall was 1.79 per cent, whilst the weighted index (wUPI) fell by 3.27 per cent. The ratio of rising to falling companies was 8:13. The UPI is being weighed down by uncertainty in the stock market and growing signs of a resumption of US strikes against Iran, while positive factors include the weather, rising demand for gas and, in the longer term, new Qatari contracts for US gas. Some interesting news emerged at the end of the week. The biggest surprise came in the form of a statement by the former CEO of Polar LNG to the Financial Times, revealing that Russia’s Novatek is behind the Alaskan project. The second piece of news concerned new LNG supply contracts signed by QatarEnergy with US and Australian companies. QatarEnergy is thus addressing the war-induced outages in its liquefaction capacity. QatarEnergy has signed two long-term deals to buy up to 4 mtpa of LNG from Cheniere Energy under agreements extending into the second half of the century, according to TradeWinds. Bloomberg first reported the news. Reuters reported on the second contract with the Australian company Woodside. A long-term deal could cover up to 3 million metric tonnes a year for 15 to 20 years, according to one source. Woodside’s Louisiana LNG plant, currently under construction, has an export capacity of 16.5 mtpa. QatarEnergy also holds a 70 per cent stake in the Golden Pass LNG facility being developed in Louisiana, which, when complete, will have the capacity to export up to 18 mtpa of LNG. Louisiana LNG is said to be asking for a premium on liquefaction fees exceeding $2.50 per mmBtu and above average US market prices due to contractual flexibility, offering potential buyers shorter contracts in return for higher prices, two people told Reuters. Reuters also reported on Thursday that QatarEnergy is in advanced talks with Venture Global (VG.N), opens new tab, regarding a long-term supply deal to purchase at least 3 million metric tonnes of LNG per year. Thirdly, Energy Intelligence reported on Qatari gas heading via the Red Sea to Poland. This is the first shipment since April. It is a Qatar-Max-sized tanker. It is worth recalling a piece of information a Czech expert shared with me. Originally, the Nord Stream pipeline was to be constructed in such a way as to prevent these ships from reaching Poland. However, the Poles realised this in time, and the Russians had to make adjustments. Energy decisions have long-term implications. The vessel’s latest Automatic Identification System (AIS) signal listed Poland’s Świnoujście import terminal as its destination, with an estimated arrival date of 14 November. This suggests the cargo is being delivered to the Polish firm Orlen under its long-term contract with QatarEnergy. However, the apparent delivery raises further questions, given that Orlen’s two separate long-term contracts with QatarEnergy are understood to remain under force majeure. The Qatari state exporter declared force majeure following the outbreak of the Gulf War and subsequent drone attacks against its Ras Laffan industrial complex in March. LNG imports from Qatar accounted for less than 10 per cent of the demand generated by Orlen and its gas customers in 2025, the company told Energy Intelligence earlier this year. A weekly Reuters round-up reported on rising gas prices in both Asia and Europe, driven by cooler weather as well as higher consumption and demand: Asian LNG prices rose to $30.50 per MMBtu, whilst European prices climbed to just over $29 per MMBtu. “Colder weather forecast across Europe in early November could accelerate storage withdrawals. Northeast Asia also faces colder-than-normal forecasts, although ample inventories should limit near-term LNG competition, with risks shifting towards later months as stocks decline,” said Kesher Sumeet, senior analyst at Energy Aspects. Asian demand has risen more sharply than European demand this week, intensifying competition between basins, said Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus. Chinese spot demand has been strong over the past week, with the state-owned CNOOC purchasing at least 11 cargoes and negotiating for further volumes in November and December to meet storage targets, whilst South Korea’s Kogas was also seeking volumes, he added. China has already experienced a sharp drop in temperatures in its northern and north-eastern regions, with temperatures forecast to fall across its central and eastern areas, whilst South Korea is also seeing colder air moving in, said Rystad Energy analyst Mathieu Utting in a note. “If this cooling proves sustained, spot LNG buying from China and South Korea will accelerate, and European buyers will need to raise their bids to secure the Atlantic cargoes they are counting on for the winter,” he said. European LNG markets rose over the week amid geopolitical developments in the Middle East, Norwegian pipeline outages and demand from Egypt, which is seeking five LNG cargoes for delivery in November, said Aly Blakeway, head of Atlantic LNG at S&P Global Energy. Spot rates rose mainly for Pacific routes, reaching $30,750 per day. Atlantic rates stood at $21,750, according to Spark Commodities. According to our UPI TCE, the average UPI contracts are now around $70,000 per day. Constituents The only double-digit gain last week was posted by ALNG (OSE: ALNG), which rose by 12 per cent. This represented a move from the lower end of the trading range to the upper end, accompanied by above-average trading volume. It must be acknowledged, however, that the average trading volume is quite low. The second-highest gain was just 4.5 per cent, posted by Tsakos Energy Navigation (NYSE: TEN). This move also took the price to the upper edge of the range and above the resistance level of the closing prices, although it ended at a key resistance level. Compared with the negative candlestick of the week before last, this is a positive candlestick (with a shadow). However, volume was only average. The trio of oil and gas companies, which also operate in the complementary LNG maritime transport sector, took the next three places in the growth rankings. Compared with the week before last, the gains were smaller. Chevron (NYSE: CVX) gained 3.65 per cent, BP (NYSE: BP) rose by 2.2 per cent and Shell (NYSE: SHEL) by 1.43 per cent. Nevertheless, all three have reached new highs for the year, well above their spring prices. Trading volumes were average to slightly below average. FLEX LNG (NYSE: FLNG) posted the only gain of more than one per cent. Although small in percentage terms, this rise is significant as it occurred at a support level following a break below the $30 mark. During the week, FLNG corrected further, down to $27, but ultimately returned above $28.50. This is a level identified and confirmed in February, July and now. Golar LNG (NASDAQ: GLNG) showed the latest positive movement. The 0.77 per cent rise followed a similar pattern to FLNG, though the support level is not as clearly visible. The price entered the range of summer 2025 prices but remained at its upper limits, perhaps even just above them. We do not know and will leave further developments to the market. ADNOC Logistics & Services (ADX: ADNOCLS) fell 7.25 per cent, ending its clearly positive run with a pullback to a lower level. Nakilat fell but staged a positive recovery, so the decline was not as severe as during the week. Nevertheless, it remains within the price range seen in 2023. Exmar continues its sideways trend slightly below its highest prices. Excelerate Energy (NYSE: EE) once again found support at $32.4. The decline was 2.4 per cent. Lines (TSE: 9104) and “K” Line (TSE: 9107) continue to move sideways near their highs for the year. Capital Clean Energy Carriers (NASDAQ: CCEC) is also trading near support within a sideways range. articles.title: EU marine protected areas: the challenge of turning the tide from paper to the sea
articles.summary: The EU’s marine protected areas often fail to receive effective protection, and the EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 marine conservation targets, according to a new report by the European Court of Auditors (ECA). Despite ambitious biodiversity commitments and a gradually expanding network of protected areas, many...
articles.body: EU marine protected areas: the challenge of turning the tide from paper to the sea in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 The EU’s marine protected areas often fail to receive effective protection, and the EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 marine conservation targets, according to a new report by the European Court of Auditors (ECA). Despite ambitious biodiversity commitments and a gradually expanding network of protected areas, many sites lack adequate conservation measures and climate adaptation planning, and report problems with staff and funding. Stakeholder involvement has become more inclusive but remains inconsistent, thus further limiting the effectiveness and long-term sustainability of marine conservation efforts. “The EU has made some progress in designating marine protected areas, but our audit shows that the true challenge is turning designation into actual protection. Turning political ambition into tangible results for marine ecosystems will require faster action, applicable protective measures, and a more coherent network across the EU’s seas,” said Iliana Ivanova, the ECA Member in charge of the audit. “To ensure that marine protected areas function effectively, we need the European Commission and member states to join forces, as well as engagement with local stakeholders.” The auditors warn that the EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 target of protecting 30 % of marine waters, with strict protection for 10 % of the total. Currently, around 14 % of EU marine waters are designated as protected, and less than 1 % as strictly protected. The auditors also found that the existing network is not working as a coherent ecological system, and that key offshore and deep-sea habitats are still inadequately protected. The fact is that designation as a marine protected area does not automatically lead to effective protection. The EU lacks a harmonised system of protection categories and corresponding activities compatible with its conservation objectives. For example, although fishing and other seabed-damaging activities pose a major threat to marine biodiversity, the auditors found that fishing restrictions apply to only a small share of protected areas. The auditors acknowledge the complexity of adopting conservation measures which affect fishing fleets from multiple member states. Nevertheless, they call for stronger cooperation at EU and national level to translate ‘marine protected area’ designations into harmonised, concrete and enforceable measures. This would also help to address funding challenges, since effective conservation requires substantial and predictable resources at a time when financing remains fragmented across national budgets and various EU instruments. The auditors warn that poor stakeholder involvement can weaken social sustainability, transparency, and public support for marine conservation measures, especially when coastal communities face significant socio-economic implications. Although member states are increasingly consulting stakeholders in more inclusive ways, they should give those who are affected more opportunities to contribute to decisions. Measures to mitigate the negative socio-economic effects of conservation measures should also be identified. The EU’s seas cover approximately 5 million km², an area larger than its landmass. About 40 % of the EU population lives within 50 km of a coast. The EU has four marine regions: the North-East Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, the Baltic Sea, and the Black Sea. These waters contain 3 648 Natura 2000 sites covering approximately 526 000 km², as well as 6 610 nationally-designated marine protected areas covering 244 000 km². More than half of the latter areas overlap with Natura 2000 sites. Special report 25/2026, “Marine protected areas – Designation alone is insufficient for meaningful protection”, is available on the ECA website, together with a one-page overview of its key facts and findings and an interactive dashboard presenting a map of EU marine protected areas. articles.body: Japan’s shipbuilders ramping up investment to double output in Shipbuilding News 27/10/2026 Japanese shipbuilders are stepping up capital investment in shipyards across the country as part of efforts to meet the government’s target of doubling domestic shipbuilding output, with the overall amount on track to exceed ¥1 trillion ($6.4 billion). A total of ¥900 billion in public- and private-sector investments have already been decided, including for the introduction of large cranes and the restoration of a dock damaged by an earthquake. Shipbuilders are eager to invest. At some shipyards, output is expected to more than double. Imabari Shipbuilding, Japan’s largest shipbuilder, plans to introduce jib cranes capable of lifting heavy loads and robots to increase steel plate-welding capacity at facilities including its headquarters in the city of Marugame, Kagawa Prefecture, and its Saijo Shipyard in the city of Saijo, Ehime Prefecture. The transport ministry has decided to provide ¥113.8 billion in subsidies to the Imabari Shipbuilding group through a fund for revitalizing the shipbuilding industry, the largest allocation yet. Total investments in the group are expected to reach around ¥300 billion. Imabari Shipbuilding said it will continually monitor production volumes as it works to double its output. Hakodate Dock, based in the city of Hakodate in Hokkaido, is moving to restore its No. 4 dock, which was rendered unusable by a major quake off southwestern Hokkaido in 1993. It plans to drain the dock to assess its condition before beginning restoration work, with shipbuilding there expected to resume around 2032. If the dock is restored, the company is expected to more than double its annual production of small bulk carriers from about five vessels in 2024. Together with investments at parent Namura Shipbuilding’s main shipyard in the city of Imari, Saga Prefecture, the two companies plan to invest up to about ¥150 billion over the next decade, including ¥49.9 billion in government aid. Kawasaki Heavy Industries, which is set to receive ¥15.6 billion in subsidies from the shipbuilding revitalization fund, plans to advance digitalization at its plant in the city of Sakaide, Kagawa Prefecture, including by introducing robots equipped with artificial intelligence. President Yasuhiko Hashimoto expressed determination to “transform shipbuilding sites” to address a shortage of workers such as skilled welders. Oshima Shipbuilding plans to install a crane and upgrade buildings at its Koyagi plant in Nagasaki, increasing its annual output of bulk carriers to about 10 vessels by around 2031, or 2.5 times the current level. As Japan’s shipbuilding industry has struggled to compete with rivals in China and South Korea, the government has designated it as one of 17 strategic fields for intensive investment. Japan aims to boost public- and private-sector investment in the industry to about ¥1 trillion by 2035 and double domestic shipbuilding output to 18 million gross tons from the 2024 level. However, the rising cost of production equipment such as cranes raises questions about whether investment plans will proceed as planned. “We greatly appreciate the government’s support, but our cash outflow is substantial,” an industry official said. “We need to scrutinize plans carefully.” Source: The Japan Times 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: India seeks South Korean expertise to boost shipbuilding, targets global top five by 2047 in Shipbuilding News 27/10/2026 India is seeking South Korean expertise in shipbuilding, manufacturing and maritime technology as it works towards becoming one of the world’s top five shipbuilding nations by 2047, Union Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said on October 25, as reported by PTI. Beginning a four-day visit to South Korea, Sonowal called on Indian professionals working in the country’s shipbuilding industry to help strengthen domestic shipyards, improve productivity and develop a skilled maritime workforce. The minister’s visit comes six months after India and South Korea adopted the VOYAGES framework to expand cooperation in shipbuilding, shipping and maritime logistics. India seeks Korean shipbuilding expertise Sonowal began his visit in Busan with an interaction involving Indian professionals associated with Samsung Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean, HD Hyundai, DNV and the Indian Register of Shipping. He urged them to use their experience in South Korea’s shipbuilding industry to support Indian companies, either by returning to India or working with them from overseas. “You can serve as living bridges between your networks in both countries,” Sonowal said, according to an official statement. The minister identified three priorities for cooperation: improving shipyard productivity and project execution, developing a globally competitive skilled workforce, and expanding partnerships in technology, manufacturing and innovation. India requires more shipbuilders, marine engineers, naval architects, designers, welders, project managers and technology specialists to support its maritime ambitions, he said. Sonowal also encouraged Indian professionals in Korea to mentor young workers and participate in initiatives such as the India Ship Technology Centre and a shipbuilding skills partnership involving the Korea International Cooperation Agency. India-South Korea shipbuilding partnership India and South Korea adopted the VOYAGES framework during South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s state visit to India in April 2026. The framework seeks to connect South Korea’s shipbuilding capabilities with India’s plans to expand shipyards, maritime manufacturing and port infrastructure. One project under the partnership is a proposed mega shipyard at Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu. An agreement signed in April between HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, National Shipbuilding & Heavy Industries Park, Tamil Nadu, and Sagarmala Finance Corporation envisages a facility with an annual capacity of 2.5 million gross tonnes. The project is expected to generate approximately 15,000 direct jobs once operations stabilise, according to a government statement issued in May. At that time, preparation of its detailed project report was underway. The government’s Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 aims to position India among the world’s five largest shipbuilding nations, with targeted annual shipbuilding output of 4.5 million gross tonnes. More industry meetings planned Sonowal is scheduled to meet shipbuilding industry leaders, maritime organisations and research institutions during his South Korea visit. “We are looking for partnership with Korea in shipbuilding, shipping, ports and maritime logistics,” he said. The minister is also scheduled to participate in a ministerial roundtable in Busan as part of the World Maritime Day Parallel Event on October 26. The discussions are expected to focus on international maritime cooperation and implementation of industry regulations. Source: Moneycontrol 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Europe Offshore Eni locks in offshore contractors for Cyprus gas project Bojan Lepic October 27, 2026 0 71 1 minute read Eni Eni Italian energy major Eni has signed the main engineering, procurement, construction, and drilling contracts for the Cronos gas development offshore Cyprus, with a string of major offshore contractors securing work on the project. The contracts, valued by local media at around $1.8bn, mark the start of the development’s execution phase in Block 6, following a final investment decision by Eni and partner TotalEnergies in July. Although Eni did not disclose the contractors involved, local media identified eight companies awarded work on the development, covering subsea production systems, pipelines, offshore installation, drilling and associated infrastructure. Baker Hughes will design, procure, and construct subsea production systems, while TechnipFMC will supply flexible gas production lines. Dalmine has been selected to supply gas export and monoethylene glycol pipelines, with Oceaneering International responsible for subsea umbilicals and control systems. China Merchants Heavy Industry will design, construct, transport, and install a floating control unit. US offshore engineering contractor McDermott will handle offshore transportation, installation, tie-ins, and commissioning of subsea pipelines and equipment. McDermott had already announced a contract worth between $500m and $750m for Cronos in September, marking its first subsea project award from Eni. Egyptian contractor Petrojet will construct a new onshore gas pipeline connecting the Zohr facilities with the Damietta LNG terminal, while Italy’s Saipem has been selected to provide drilling services using its Saipem 10000 drillship. Separately, Halliburton secured a bundled well construction and completions contract for Cronos in September, covering drilling fluids, directional drilling, cementing, automation, and other well services. The Cronos development will involve four subsea wells targeting resources estimated at more than 3trn cubic feet of gas initially in place. Production is expected to begin in the first half of 2028, reaching a plateau of up to 500m standard cubic feet per day. Gas will be transported to Egypt for processing through existing Zohr-field infrastructure before being liquefied at Damietta for export, primarily to European markets. Eni operates Block 6 with a 50% stake, while TotalEnergies holds the remaining interest. articles.title: Container freight rates diverge as global benchmarks rise and Asian indexes weaken
articles.summary: Global container freight rates delivered a mixed performance in the latest weekly assessments, with major international benchmarks moving higher while Chinese freight indexes showed more subdued results. The divergence was particularly evident on Asia-Europe routes, where Drewry reported further increases but the...
articles.body: Global container freight rates delivered a mixed performance in the latest weekly assessments, with major international benchmarks moving higher while Chinese freight indexes showed more subdued results. The divergence was particularly evident on Asia-Europe routes, where Drewry reported further increases but the NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) continued to decline. Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) rose 2% to US$4,585 per 40-foot container, reaching its highest level in 15 weeks. The Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) also advanced, increasing 5% to US$3,560. Meanwhile, the China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) declined, while the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) registered marginal gains. The latest figures highlight an uneven freight market, with movements varying considerably across benchmarks and individual trade lanes. Chinese freight indexes show limited momentum The SCFI edged up 0.05% to 3,681.34 points on 23 October, compared with 3,679.58 in the previous assessment. The marginal increase indicates broadly stable conditions in the index. The CCFI moved in the opposite direction, declining approximately 2.41% to 1,876.27 points from 1,922.64 a week earlier. It was the most pronounced movement among the three Chinese composite indexes. The NCFI increased approximately 0.50% to 2,509.30 points, compared with 2,496.79 in the preceding assessment. Together, these readings present a mixed picture. While SCFI and NCFI remained in positive territory, their gains were considerably smaller than those recorded by the FBX and Drewry WCI. NYFI records further Asia-Europe weakness The NYFI assessment published on 23 October showed contrasting developments across the five monitored trade lanes. On the Transpacific, Asia-US West Coast increased 1.39% to 7,579.09, compared with 7,475.40 a week earlier. Asia-US East Coast remained virtually unchanged, declining 0.02% to 9,936.89 from 9,938.75. The figures indicate relatively stable Transpacific conditions, with modest improvement on the West Coast and little movement on the East Coast. Asia-North Europe continued to weaken, declining 2.53% to 3,039.67 from 3,118.71. The latest decrease followed a 7.08% decline in the previous assessment, extending the downward movement on the route. The Transatlantic market recorded sharper declines. Westbound rates fell 7.30% to 2,882.09 from 3,109.16, partially reversing the previous week’s 14.77% increase. Eastbound rates experienced an even steeper reduction, dropping 19.28% to 946.64 from 1,172.79. This followed an 8.53% decrease in the preceding assessment. The two Transatlantic movements were among the most significant developments in the latest NYFI readings, illustrating substantial week-to-week volatility. Drewry WCI reaches a 15-week high Drewry’s WCI increased 2% to US$4,585 per 40-foot container on 22 October, marking its second consecutive weekly increase and highest level in 15 weeks. On the Transpacific, Shanghai-Los Angeles rose 2% to US$8,007 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-New York increased 1% to US$10,166. Asia-Europe routes also recorded further gains. Shanghai-Rotterdam increased 3% to US$3,632, while Shanghai-Genoa climbed 5% to US$4,152. According to Drewry, carriers have announced eight blank sailings on Asia-Europe services for the following week, compared with two in the current week. The consultancy linked the increase in cancelled sailings to efforts to manage available capacity and support freight rates. On the Transpacific, announced blank sailings declined from six to two. Drewry expects rates on these routes to remain broadly stable, while anticipating a slight increase on Asia-Europe. These expectations remain forecasts rather than confirmed future market movements. FBX Global Index posts stronger growth The FBX Global Container Freight Index increased 5% to US$3,560, compared with approximately US$3,397 in the previous weekly reading. The increase was stronger than the 2% advance recorded in the preceding assessment, indicating continued upward movement in the global benchmark. The FBX and WCI therefore both recorded gains for a second consecutive week, although their respective increases differed. Their positive performance contrasts with the decline in the CCFI and the limited changes recorded by the SCFI and NCFI. Asia-Europe remains the main point of divergence One of the clearest differences in the latest assessments concerns Asia-Europe freight rates. Drewry reported increases of 3% on Shanghai-Rotterdam and 5% on Shanghai-Genoa, extending the recovery recorded in its previous assessment. In contrast, NYFI Asia-North Europe declined 2.53%, following a substantially larger decrease a week earlier. The difference is important but should not be interpreted as a direct contradiction. NYFI and Drewry apply different methodologies and reporting periods, while their route definitions and underlying rate assessments are not identical. The NYFI is based on reported transactions involving containers that have actually shipped, whereas Drewry’s WCI provides assessed spot freight rate benchmarks. Consequently, the two indexes can report different short-term movements within related markets. Market outlook The latest assessments suggest that the recovery in global container freight benchmarks has continued, but its strength varies considerably across the market. Drewry’s WCI and the FBX recorded further increases, supported by stronger readings on several major East-West routes. However, the decline in the CCFI and the limited gains in the SCFI and NCFI indicate that the improvement is not uniform across Chinese freight benchmarks. Asia-Europe remains a key area to monitor, particularly as Drewry anticipates tighter capacity following an increase in announced blank sailings. On the Transpacific, NYFI and Drewry point to broadly stable or moderately firmer conditions, although the extent of improvement differs between routes. Meanwhile, the sharp declines in both Transatlantic directions reported by NYFI underline the volatility affecting individual markets. The next weekly assessments will provide a clearer indication of whether the recent increases in global benchmarks can be sustained and whether the differing Asia-Europe readings begin to converge.
takeaways: Global container freight rates delivered a mixed performance in the latest weekly assessments, with major international benchmarks moving higher while Chinese freight indexes showed more subdued results.
The divergence was particularly evident on Asia-Europe routes, where Drewry reported further increases but the NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) continued to decline.
Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) rose 2% to US$4,585 per 40-foot container, reaching its highest level in 15 weeks.

articles.body: Middle East Operations Asyad Group prices $132m shipping stake sale Adis Ajdin October 27, 2026 0 106 1 minute read Asyad Shipping Asyad Shipping Oman’s Asyad Group has priced an institutional share sale in its listed shipping subsidiary at OMR50.8m ($132m), reducing its ownership as part of a move to broaden the company’s shareholder base. Muscat-listed Asyad Shipping said the institutional bookbuilding process closed heavily oversubscribed. The transaction covers 5% of Asyad Shipping’s issued share capital. Upon completion, the company’s free float will rise to 25%, meeting the minimum requirement set by Oman’s Financial Services Authority. The shares are being sold by parent Asyad Group, which will receive the proceeds. No new shares are being issued, and Asyad Shipping will not receive any of the funds. The group is also preparing a separate retail offering of up to 1.25% of the shipping company at the same price, subject to regulatory approval. Settlement and listing of the institutional shares are expected on November 4. The remaining shares held by Asyad Group will be subject to a 180-day lock-up following settlement. The transaction follows Asyad Shipping’s March 2025 initial public offering, which raised approximately $333m and brought 20% of the company into public ownership. Since listing, the company has continued expanding and renewing its fleet across the tanker, dry bulk, gas and container sectors. Asyad operated a fleet of 91 vessels at the end of June, including 48 owned or co-owned ships, 31 chartered-in vessels and 12 newbuildings. articles.body: Fugro Secures UXO Survey and Clearance Work for German Offshore Grid Links Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 (Credit: Fugro) Fugro has secured a contract from 50Hertz to carry out unexploded ordnance (UXO) survey, identification and clearance work for the LanWin3 and LanWin6 offshore grid connection projects in the German sector of the North Sea. The work will help prepare cable routes for the installation of high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables connecting offshore wind farms to Germany's electricity network. The two grid connections will each have a transmission capacity of up to 2 GW, providing a combined capacity of 4 GW to deliver offshore wind power to the national grid. Starting in the second quarter of 2027, Fugro will survey 200-meter-wide corridors along the LanWin3 and LanWin6 routes using two Geowing fixed magnetic gradiometer arrays, each equipped with ten magnetic sensors. The systems will detect potential unexploded ordnance and other objects on or beneath the seabed, generating data to map potential hazards and establish a master target list for further investigation. Follow-on inspection and identification activities are scheduled for 2028, using remotely operated vehicle (ROV) technology and specialist detection systems to investigate selected targets and remove debris where required. Fugro will also support the removal and disposal of confirmed unexploded ordnance in accordance with regulatory requirements, helping prepare the cable corridors for installation. “On a project of this scale, the challenge is that the number and nature of potential UXO can only be known once the survey is complete. Building a reliable picture of the seabed at an early stage will allow 50Hertz to plan the next steps with greater certainty and manage safety throughout the cable installation program,” said Ronny Bøhn, Fugro’s Director of Marine Geophysics for Europe and Africa.

articles.title: What cargo shipping can learn from cruise about crewing technology
articles.summary: Raal Harris, the founder of PitchFrame, brings readers details of an interesting session from last week’s Crew Connect Global in Manila. We spend a lot of time in cargo shipping looking to aviation for inspiration in approaches to safety, technology, training and operational efficiency. But there’s another industry...
articles.body: Contributions Operations Tech What cargo shipping can learn from cruise about crewing technology Splash October 27, 2026 0 220 7 minutes read Associated British Ports Associated British Ports Raal Harris, the founder of PitchFrame, brings readers details of an interesting session from last week’s Crew Connect Global in Manila. We spend a lot of time in cargo shipping looking to aviation for inspiration in approaches to safety, technology, training and operational efficiency. But there’s another industry sitting much closer to home that perhaps deserves more of our attention: cruise. At Crew Connect Global in Manila, I had the opportunity to explore this theme with four people who understand the cruise sector from very different perspectives: Eric Visser of Holland America Line and Seabourn, Anca Preda of Columbia Shipmanagement, Calypso Diareme of ATPI and Joost van Ree of Nevetal. Our question was straightforward: what can cargo shipping actually learn from the way cruise manages its crew, and particularly from the technology that supports it? The discussion revealed some important differences, but also some surprisingly transferable lessons. And while cruise may be further ahead in certain aspects of crew management technology, the most interesting differences aren’t necessarily the systems themselves. They’re what those systems enable organisations to do. Different scale, different challenges We should start by acknowledging that cruise and cargo operate under very different conditions. Eric Visser explained that Holland America Line and Seabourn employ around 16,000 people across their fleet, with between 10 and 40 crew joining or leaving individual vessels almost every day. A large cruise ship might carry 1,000 or even 2,000 crew, compared with perhaps 20 to 25 on a typical cargo vessel. Then there’s predictability. Cruise operators can know 18 to 24 months in advance where their ships will be, often down to the hour. That makes workforce planning, crew changes and training considerably easier to organise than in cargo shipping, where schedules and port calls are subject to disruption at a moment’s notice. But scale and predictability aren’t the only differences. Cruise ships have entire departments dedicated to HR, training and employee welfare. They manage complex workforces covering everything from navigation and engineering to hospitality, entertainment and catering. And the people working in those departments are directly responsible for delivering the product that customers have paid for. As Eric memorably put it, “Our cargo talks back to us.” A passenger’s experience is shaped by the people they encounter, and poor performance can translate almost immediately into customer dissatisfaction and reputational damage that impacts the bottom line. That creates a very visible commercial incentive to invest in the workforce. Cargo shipping has equally important dependencies on the competence, wellbeing and performance of its seafarers, but the relationship with commercial performance is often less immediate and less visible. This distinction helps explain why cruise has developed some of its approaches to crew management. It also raises the first important question for cargo: are we giving our people the strategic attention their contribution deserves? Building a workforce, not just filling vacancies One of the most interesting distinctions Eric made concerned the relationship between ship operators and the organisations that supply their crew. In his organisation, they don’t refer to manning agents. They call them talent partners. That might sound like a cosmetic change, but the thinking behind it is significant. A traditional crewing transaction starts with a vacancy. The operator needs a third engineer, the agency identifies a qualified candidate, and that person joins the ship. In cruise, Eric described a much more continuous relationship, where the recruitment partner shares responsibility for supporting the seafarer throughout their employment, including their wellbeing, development and career progression. “We’re really building a workforce rather than that we are building a portfolio of people,” he explained. The distinction is important. One approach is principally concerned with meeting today’s crewing requirements. The other is concerned with developing the people and capabilities the organisation will need tomorrow. Anca Preda reinforced this point, explaining that cruise has developed a much broader maritime HR function, with greater emphasis on employee engagement, employer branding, talent development and retention. “We don’t look at talent attraction as an administrative function,” she told us. Of course, a cargo vessel cannot accommodate a dedicated onboard HR department. But Anca argued that this needn’t prevent cargo operators from adopting the underlying approach. These responsibilities can be managed from shore, provided the organisation establishes the right relationships, processes and accountability. This is perhaps the first genuinely transferable lesson. Strategic workforce management doesn’t depend on having thousands of employees on a vessel. It depends on recognising that recruitment, development, deployment and retention are connected activities rather than separate administrative tasks. What the data tells us about people Of course planning and coordination at this scale require technology and data that can support a more strategic approach. Eric offered an excellent example. His organisation had experienced turnover of around 30% within one group of officers. The natural assumption was that remuneration was the problem. But when they examined the available workforce information, they discovered that the more significant issue was a bottleneck in career progression. People couldn’t see a route to promotion. Addressing that problem reduced turnover. It’s a simple example, but an important one. Without the data, the organisation might have responded by increasing pay, potentially at considerable expense, without resolving the underlying issue. Cruise operators are increasingly connecting information about recruitment, competence, training, career progression, deployment and retention to build a more complete picture of their workforce. This also creates opportunities to take a more sophisticated approach to professional development. Eric described how cross-training allows people to move between departments and progress through different roles. Rather than viewing an individual solely in terms of the job they currently perform, the organisation considers their existing competencies, their potential and the additional development needed to prepare them for another role. Anca described exploring how AI might automate part of this process, comparing role requirements, identifying competency gaps and suggesting the training needed to support career progression. That is a much more interesting application of AI than simply making existing administrative processes faster. It could help organisations understand not only whether they have enough people, but whether they are developing the right capabilities for future requirements. There is, however, an important prerequisite. Joost van Ree pointed out that some cruise operators already have relatively mature data platforms, developed initially to support commercial functions such as reservations, finance and customer satisfaction. Connecting crew management, learning and other operational systems to those platforms creates opportunities for more predictive workforce planning. Cargo shipping, by contrast, often still relies heavily on spreadsheets, PDFs and disconnected systems. The challenge isn’t necessarily a lack of data. It’s the inability to bring that information together into something sufficiently reliable to support decisions. And that matters even more as organisations begin to introduce AI. Predictive systems are only as useful as the information on which they depend. When planning meets reality Perhaps the most striking operational example came from Calypso Diareme, who works across both cruise and cargo crew logistics at ATPI. She described the challenges of managing crew movements during the recent Middle East crisis. ATPI had to arrange the evacuation of several thousand cruise crew, alongside much smaller numbers of cargo seafarers requiring changes to their travel arrangements. According to Calypso, the cruise movements were completed within days, while some of the cargo movements took weeks. The difference wasn’t simply the availability of technology. Cruise operators had developed processes following COVID that allowed the various parties involved to work from connected information. They knew who needed to travel, what documentation those individuals held, which routes were available, who needed to be involved and what alternatives existed when plans changed. In cargo, individual crew changes were more likely to be treated as separate cases, requiring people to gather information and coordinate arrangements afresh. This is a particularly useful illustration of what digital maturity actually means. A crew-change platform might optimise a travel itinerary, but that is of limited value if the crewing department, travel provider, port agent and vessel are working from different information. Similarly, an algorithm might identify the ideal person for an assignment, but that doesn’t help much if the person cannot reach the ship. The value comes from connecting the whole process, from workforce planning through to successful embarkation, and ensuring that people can respond effectively when something goes wrong. Technology enables that coordination, but it cannot substitute for the processes, relationships and human judgement needed to make it work. For cargo operators, where crew changes are often less predictable, that capability may be particularly valuable. Don’t copy cruise. Learn from it. There is a temptation, when looking at a more technologically mature operation, to assume that the answer is to acquire the same systems, but that is not necessarily the case. Cruise operators have scale, operational characteristics and commercial incentives that can justify investments which would make little sense for many cargo fleets. And cruise itself isn’t a single model. Expedition vessels, river cruise operators and smaller luxury ships face different challenges from the largest ocean-going cruise vessels. Joost’s closing advice was particularly sensible: “Don’t overspend chasing cruise-level solutions.” The opportunity is to adopt the principles that make those solutions effective, rather than replicate their complexity. That might mean connecting existing workforce data before investing in new AI applications. It might mean developing a clearer understanding of competency and promotion readiness rather than simply tracking training completion. Or it might mean redesigning crew-change processes so that information can move reliably between the organisations involved. It also means giving maritime HR a stronger voice in operational and commercial decision-making. As Eric argued, HR should be regarded as a strategic partner in the development of the business, not simply the function responsible for supplying people. None of this requires cargo shipping to become more like cruise in its wider operating model. It requires us to think differently about how we use technology to manage, support and develop the people on whom our operations depend. My biggest takeaway from the discussion was that cruise’s advantage isn’t simply that it has more sophisticated technology. In many cases, it has developed a more connected approach to workforce management, supported by better information, clearer processes and a stronger understanding of the commercial value of its people. And that is something cargo shipping can learn from, regardless of fleet size. articles.body: GXO Logistics and Agility Robotics have announced plans to expand their partnership by deploying humanoid robots at two additional logistics facilities in the United States. The expansion will bring Agility Robotics’ Digit robots to GXO warehouses in Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee. Deployments are expected to begin in early 2027, supporting e-commerce fulfillment and repetitive material-handling tasks. The announcement, made on October 26, builds on the companies’ existing commercial partnership. Their collaboration has already demonstrated the use of humanoid robots in active warehouse operations. At GXO’s Flowery Branch facility in Georgia, Digit robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since their initial deployment. The robots work alongside existing warehouse automation, transferring containers and placing them onto conveyor systems. The latest agreement marks a further step towards expanding humanoid robotics beyond a single operating site. GXO expands commercial use of humanoid robots GXO and Agility Robotics began collaborating in late 2023 through a proof-of-concept project at the Flowery Branch warehouse. In June 2024, the companies signed a multi-year Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS) agreement. This introduced Digit robots into live warehouse operations under a commercial arrangement. The deployment also included Agility Arc, a cloud-based platform designed to manage robot fleets and integrate them with warehouse systems. Since then, the companies have continued developing the technology through practical operational experience. “Innovation is most powerful when it delivers practical solutions that create value for our customers and our people,” said Patrick Kelleher, CEO of GXO. Kelleher explained that the partnership has focused on turning emerging technology into operational improvements. He also highlighted the potential of humanoid robots to support employees and customers. The next phase will introduce Digit 4 robots at the two additional GXO facilities. The companies then plan to transition to Digit 5 once the newer model becomes commercially available. Digit 5, unveiled in September 2026, is designed to operate safely alongside people and perform a wider range of industrial tasks. Agility Robotics prepares for wider commercial deployment The expansion comes as Agility Robotics increases its efforts to support larger commercial deployments. Across its commercial operations and customer programmes, Digit has accumulated more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation. According to the company, this experience has helped shape the development of its next-generation robots. “GXO was the first customer to put Digit to work in live operations under a commercial agreement, and expanding to additional sites is the clearest signal that the value is real,” said Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility Robotics. Johnson added that customers are increasingly focusing on where humanoid robots can be deployed at scale rather than whether the technology can operate in warehouses. The carrier stressed that no weather-related operational disruptions have been reported at this stage. However, forecasts indicate above-average rainfall across much of the country. Potential impact on cargo operations Severe weather could affect operations at the Port of Mombasa and disrupt inland cargo movements. Possible impacts include delays to vessel operations, terminal access and container handling. Road and rail services could also face disruption, including cargo moving along the Northern Corridor and transit shipments to Uganda. Import collections, export gate-ins, cargo deliveries and empty-container returns may experience delays. Hapag-Lloyd also highlighted an increased risk of water or moisture damage during cargo handling and transportation. Precautions for customers Hapag-Lloyd advised customers to allow additional time for cargo movements and arrange collections and deliveries as early as possible. Shippers should inspect containers before stuffing and report any visible damage, leaks or moisture. Cargo should also receive adequate protection from rain during packing, storage and transportation. Customers should monitor vessel schedules and cut-off times. They should also coordinate closely with transport providers and clearing agents. Hapag-Lloyd said it will monitor weather developments alongside port, terminal and inland transportation partners. The carrier will provide further updates if significant operational disruptions occur.

articles.title: Wall Street splits over tanker boom
articles.summary: Wall Street’s increasingly divided outlook for the tanker supercycle has taken another twist, with investment bank Evercore ISI dramatically raising its freight forecasts and share price targets while warning that the industry’s extraordinary earnings could be approaching their peak. In research published yesterday,...
articles.body: Americas Tankers Wall Street splits over tanker boom Sam Chambers October 27, 2026 0 887 3 minutes read Photo by Aditya Vyas on Unsplash Photo by Aditya Vyas on Unsplash Wall Street’s increasingly divided outlook for the tanker supercycle has taken another twist, with investment bank Evercore ISI dramatically raising its freight forecasts and share price targets while warning that the industry’s extraordinary earnings could be approaching their peak. In research published yesterday, Jonathan Chappell of Evercore doubled his 2027 VLCC earnings forecast from $57,500 to $115,000 a day, while raising his 2026 projection by 97% to $215,000. The bank now anticipates fourth-quarter VLCC spot earnings averaging an extraordinary $476,000 a day on its modelled basis, before rates begin retreating through 2027. Yet Chappell remains cautious about chasing tanker shares, warning that the market is being sustained by exceptional geopolitical disruption rather than conventional supply-demand fundamentals. The seven tanker companies under Evercore’s coverage have gained between 72% and 154% this year, comfortably outperforming the broader stock market. Chappell argued that tanker equities have effectively become a leveraged bet on continued Middle East instability, with their direction increasingly determined by geopolitical headlines rather than historical valuation metrics. The bank has lifted its Frontline price target from $41 to $53 but maintains an in-line rating, considerably below BTIG’s $70 target. Evercore also raised its DHT target from $19 to $26, while retaining an in-line rating, and it increased its Nordic American Tankers target to $7 while maintaining an underperform recommendation. The bank sees better relative value in product tanker owners, including Scorpio Tankers, Torm and Ardmore Shipping, which it considers less vulnerable to an eventual normalisation of crude tanker earnings and asset prices. Other Wall Street analysts remain more optimistic about the duration of the boom. BTIG’s Greg Lewis continues to favour tanker equities, arguing that depleted oil inventories and prolonged disruption could sustain exceptional earnings. B. Riley Securities recently raised its International Seaways target to $140, while Jefferies said recently it believes tanker earnings will decline more slowly than investors anticipate. Jefferies puts average VLCC earnings at $65,000 a day in 2027, pointing to an ageing fleet and the potential for substantial inventory restocking. Its lower numerical forecast than Evercore’s illustrates how differences in freight assumptions do not necessarily translate into the same conclusions about equity valuations. Shipbrokers, meanwhile, are increasingly identifying warning signs. Braemar reported exorbitant freight costs are encouraging Asian refiners to source shorter-haul Middle Eastern crude rather than Atlantic barrels, undermining tonne-mile demand. Affinity similarly reported a VLCC correction, although suezmax and aframax markets remain exceptionally strong. Evercore identified another worrying development: its average forecast for global oil demand growth this year has deteriorated to a contraction of 1.75m barrels a day. The bank notes that the only other annual oil demand contractions over the past three decades came in 2009 and 2020, both followed by extremely difficult tanker markets. The supply picture is equally troubling. Drawing on Clarksons data, Evercore forecasts tanker newbuilding deliveries of 50.1m dwt next year, rising to an unprecedented 62.8m dwt in 2028, with another 54.9m dwt scheduled for 2029 It calculates underlying net tanker fleet growth of 5.3% this year and 5.5% in 2027, before accounting for disruption-related inefficiencies. Hartland Shipping Services separately forecasts more than 100 VLCC deliveries annually in both 2028 and 2029, levels last witnessed during the 1970s supertanker boom. BRS counts 283 VLCC orders scheduled for delivery from 2028 onwards. Yet scrapping remains negligible. Banchero Costa records just four VLCC demolitions during the first nine months of 2026, despite an ageing fleet. The market’s extraordinary distortions are also spilling into the courts. Commodity trader Mercuria’s challenge to the Baltic Exchange’s Gulf-China VLCC benchmark is now underway in London, questioning the reliability of assessments during the Hormuz crisis. The Baltic disputes the allegations. Evercore warned yesterday that shipping costs are now approaching 25% to 30% of the value of the oil being transported, creating the risk that high freight rates themselves destroy demand. The bank nevertheless acknowledges that predicting the timing of any reversal is extraordinarily difficult. articles.title: SAT-JAM: Ships must learn to navigate without GPS
articles.summary: A researcher in Denmark who has developed a new system for tracking satellite navigation interference from space has a stark warning for the shipping industry in today’s Maritime CEO interview: GPS can no longer be considered a dependable means of navigation. Kian Bostani Nezhad, a PhD researcher at the Technical...
articles.body: Europe Maritime CEO Operations Tech SAT-JAM: Ships must learn to navigate without GPS Splash October 27, 2026 0 1,753 2 minutes read A researcher in Denmark who has developed a new system for tracking satellite navigation interference from space has a stark warning for the shipping industry in today’s Maritime CEO interview: GPS can no longer be considered a dependable means of navigation. Kian Bostani Nezhad, a PhD researcher at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), believes the maritime industry needs a fundamental rethink of its reliance on satellite positioning. “GNSS interference has become a perpetual problem,” he tells Maritime CEO. “Everyone who uses GNSS must change their mindset from GNSS being a primary and dependable navigation solution, to it being a supplement to other navigation methods.” Nezhad is the creator of SAT-JAM, a freely accessible online platform launched in September that maps GNSS interference detected by satellites orbiting hundreds of kilometres above Earth. The project began with an unexpected conversation last year. “I heard a spacecraft operator complain about their spacecraft having problems with GNSS over Europe,” he recalls. Intrigued, Nezhad searched for publicly available navigation data collected by low-Earth-orbit satellites and discovered several European Space Agency missions providing the information. Every mission he examined showed evidence of interference. Nezhad then submitted a research abstract to the Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies conference in March, before developing SAT-JAM, inspired by GPSJam, a website tracking interference experienced by aircraft. His findings demonstrate that disruption affecting ships in the Baltic, Black Sea and other maritime hotspots is not confined to the Earth’s surface. Satellites operating 400 to 600 km above the planet can also experience degraded positioning signals. The platform uses publicly available European Sentinel satellite data, updated as new observations become available, to identify where spacecraft experience interference. However, Nezhad stresses an important distinction between detecting interference and locating its source. “SAT-JAM does not show where GNSS interference originates from, but where spacecraft measure the GNSS interference,” he explains. “The actual source, and the measurement can be far apart, due to the high altitude of satellites.” The distinction matters for shipowners attempting to understand the geographical spread of jamming and spoofing. Satellite measurements cannot automatically be interpreted as evidence of interference affecting vessels directly beneath them. Nezhad’s research background also includes maritime surveillance. His master’s thesis explored applying facial recognition algorithms to satellite imagery to identify and re-identify individual ships. Asked what practical advice he would offer shipowners facing increasingly unreliable satellite navigation, Nezhad identifies two priorities. First, operators should keep pace with improvements in GNSS receiver technology, particularly controlled reception pattern antennas (CRPA), which can suppress interfering signals. His second recommendation is more fundamental – seafarers must learn to navigate without GNSS. “I know it is easier said than done, but GNSS interference has become a perpetual problem,” he stresses. Britain warned shipowners earlier this month that satellite navigation can no longer be relied upon in major shipping regions, urging crews to practise operating without GPS. New guidance from the Maritime and Coastguard Agency highlights growing jamming and spoofing threats across the Baltic, Black Sea, Middle East Gulf and East Asia, affecting everything from ECDIS and AIS to autopilots and port systems. Maritime intelligence firm Windward recorded an average of 5,131 daily jamming incidents during the third quarter. The MCA recommends regular navigation drills, alternative positioning methods and greater awareness of equipment vulnerabilities.
