articles.body: Americas Greater China Regulatory US moves to extend China ship fee truce into 2027 Adis Ajdin October 27, 2026 0 395 1 minute read Port of Long Beach Port of Long Beach The United States is looking to extend its suspension of additional port fees targeting China-linked shipping for another two months, keeping the measures on hold until January 9, 2027, while trade negotiations with Beijing continue. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has opened a public consultation on a proposal to prolong the suspension from November 10, when the current arrangement expires. Under the proposed extension, operators would continue to be exempt from the additional maritime transport charges introduced under Washington’s Section 301 investigation into China’s dominance of shipping, logistics and shipbuilding. The proposal would also maintain the suspension of separate duties on certain cargo-handling equipment. The US initially introduced the vessel charges in October 2025, targeting Chinese-owned and operated ships, Chinese-built tonnage operated by non-Chinese companies and certain foreign-built vehicle carriers. The measures prompted widespread changes to fleet deployment plans, with owners and operators looking to limit their exposure to the additional costs. Washington and Beijing subsequently agreed to suspend their respective maritime charges for one year as part of a broader trade agreement, with the American suspension taking effect on November 10, 2025. Splash’s earlier coverage tracked the potential impact on major container carriers, including estimates that COSCO and OOCL could face billions of dollars in additional costs if the charges remained in place. The latest proposal would provide another two months for negotiations without restoring the charges. USTR has set an October 30 deadline for public comments before deciding whether to proceed. articles.summary: The Port of Long Beach has released a revised draft supplemental environmental impact report for its Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility project, reflecting proposed design modifications to one of the port’s major rail infrastructure developments.v Announced on October 23, 2026, the recirculated environmental study...
articles.body: The Port of Long Beach has released a revised draft supplemental environmental impact report for its Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility project, reflecting proposed design modifications to one of the port’s major rail infrastructure developments.v Announced on October 23, 2026, the recirculated environmental study examines changes involving rail infrastructure, utility connections, construction staging areas and nearby road facilities. The most significant proposed modification involves the complete demolition of the Berths D52–D54 transit shed to accommodate the realignment of Pico Avenue. The building has been determined eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places, making its proposed demolition an important consideration in the project’s environmental review. The latest study follows an earlier draft released in September 2025, which examined the possibility of reconfiguring the existing transit shed rather than removing it entirely. However, subsequent engineering assessments determined that partial demolition would not be economically or physically feasible without damaging the remaining structure. Pier B project aims to expand on-dock rail capacity The Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility is designed to improve the movement of containers between marine terminals and the national rail network, reducing reliance on trucks for cargo transportation. According to the Port of Long Beach, the completed facility is expected to triple its on-dock rail capacity and reduce rail dwell times from approximately four days to 24 hours by 2032. These improvements are intended to strengthen the port’s operational efficiency, support cargo growth and contribute to its environmental objectives. Construction of the wider Pier B project began in 2024, with completion currently expected in 2032. The proposed modifications outlined in the revised environmental study also include adjustments to railway tracks, installation or removal of utilities, additional construction staging and equipment areas, pavement restriping and signage changes. Sections of Grant Street and Southern Pacific Drive in Wilmington would also be closed as part of the proposed changes. The modifications are being assessed through the supplemental environmental review process and should not be considered completed construction activities. Public consultation continues on revised plans The Port of Long Beach has opened a new public consultation period to gather feedback on the revised environmental assessment. A virtual public meeting is scheduled for November 18, 2026, allowing stakeholders and community members to review the proposed modifications and provide input. Written comments will be accepted until December 9, 2026. The revised draft supplemental environmental impact report is available through the port’s environmental review website. The Pier B project forms part of the Port of Long Beach’s broader infrastructure development programme, which aims to strengthen freight rail connectivity and accommodate future container traffic growth. By increasing the proportion of containers transported directly by rail, the port expects to reduce truck movements and improve the efficiency of cargo transfers between its marine terminals and inland destinations. The latest environmental review represents a further planning step for the ongoing project, rather than the announcement of a new rail development or additional capacity beyond the existing Pier B programme.

articles.title: Hambantota Port sees new opportunities as container ships return to Suez
articles.summary: Hambantota International Port Group (HIPG) expects a sustained return of container shipping through the Red Sea and Suez Canal to create new commercial opportunities for the Sri Lankan port, as it prepares to expand its container handling capabilities. The port operator believes that the restoration of the...
articles.body: Hambantota International Port Group (HIPG) expects a sustained return of container shipping through the Red Sea and Suez Canal to create new commercial opportunities for the Sri Lankan port, as it prepares to expand its container handling capabilities. The port operator believes that the restoration of the established East–West shipping corridor could strengthen Hambantota’s position in regional transshipment networks, while supporting demand for bunkering, ship supplies and other marine services. The outlook follows an October 2026 assessment by maritime consultancy Linerlytica, which forecasts a full-scale return of container shipping to the Suez route by the first quarter of 2027. However, the pace of any recovery remains dependent on security conditions and individual shipping lines’ operational decisions. Located approximately ten nautical miles from the main East–West shipping route, Hambantota is seeking to capitalise on its geographical position as carriers reconsider diversions around the Cape of Good Hope. Suez recovery could support Hambantota’s container ambitions According to HIPG, disruptions in the Red Sea initially accelerated the development of Hambantota’s container transshipment business, as congestion at the Port of Colombo created demand for additional handling capacity. The port began accommodating overflow cargo in April 2024 and launched its inaugural MSC container transshipment service on April 9 of that year. “The Red Sea disruption advanced our container project. Congestion in Colombo Port created a requirement for additional capacity, and we began accommodating overflow cargo with the resources available to us in April 2024,” said Bindu Ranasinghe, General Manager – Commercial and Marketing at HIPG. “That experience encouraged us to proceed with a full-scale operation and further investment. With expanded capacity coming into place, we welcome the prospect of shipping returning more fully to the Suez route,” Ranasinghe added. As part of its expansion programme, HIPG has committed US$149 million to new container handling equipment, with annual container handling capacity targeted to reach two million TEUs during the first quarter of 2027. The company expects that a sustained return to the Suez corridor could make Hambantota more attractive to shipping lines operating between Asia and Europe. “When vessels use the established East–West route through Suez, they pass much closer to Hambantota. We have used the period of disruption to expand our capabilities, and a sustained return to that route would give us a stronger opportunity to attract business,” Ranasinghe said. Beyond container transshipment, HIPG anticipates additional opportunities in bunkering and vessel support services as more shipping activity potentially shifts back towards the traditional route. Gateway cargo and regional connections form part of growth strategy HIPG is also seeking to diversify Hambantota’s container business by developing gateway cargo for Sri Lankan importers and exporters, alongside its existing transshipment operations. The port’s industrial park, nearby Board of Investment zones and proposed industrial developments are expected to support the establishment of a domestic cargo base. A planned container inspection centre is intended to facilitate gateway operations, with benefits anticipated from the first quarter of 2027. “To attract more shipping lines and services, we also need gateway cargo,” Ranasinghe said. “Industrial development within and around the port, together with the inspection facilities we are establishing, will help create the conditions for that business to grow.” Meanwhile, HIPG is assessing the longer-term potential of alternative cargo connections developed during disruptions affecting access to ports in the Persian Gulf. Hambantota has handled transshipment cargo for onward feeder services to accessible regional ports, providing alternative arrangements for shipping lines and their customers. Although improved access to Gulf ports could lead some cargo to return to previous routes, HIPG believes that existing commercial commitments, service networks, insurance conditions and security considerations will influence future decisions. “Shipping lines and their customers have established alternative arrangements, and those networks will not necessarily change immediately,” Ranasinghe said. The company maintains that connections established through Hambantota could remain commercially relevant even as regional shipping conditions improve. HIPG’s broader strategy is to combine container transshipment, gateway cargo, industrial development and marine services to establish a more diversified business as shipping networks across the region evolve.

articles.title: As Attacks Mount, Shipping Faces an Uncomfortable Question: Are Safety Rules Fit for War?
articles.summary: October has become the worst month on record for attacks on merchant ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz, and oil is now washing onto the beaches of the United Arab Emirates.

Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS By Paul Morgan (gCaptain) – October has become the worst month on record for attacks on merchant ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz, and oil is now washing onto the beaches of the United Arab Emirates. The engineering question that follows is uncomfortable: were the ships under fire ever designed, equipped or crewed to survive what is happening to them? On 23 October, Reuters reported data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy recording 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait and surrounding waterways during October, and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on 28 February. The institute has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017, and October tops its records. The IMO’s own list records around 120 incidents in the Strait and the wider Middle East since the conflict started, while UKMTO had logged 135 conflict-related incidents by 16 October. The totals differ because coverage and methods differ, and UKMTO reporting is voluntary, but the direction of travel is beyond dispute. The damage to the tanker fleet is striking. A Reuters review of IMO and MarineTraffic data found that more than 30 very large crude carriers had been damaged, including 11 in October alone, equivalent to around 3.5% of the world’s VLCC fleet. Greek risk consultancy Marisks counted a dozen ships attacked between 5 and 11 October, the highest weekly total of the conflict. The human cost has been heavy. By September the IMO counted at least 22 seafarers killed in 80 verified attacks around Hormuz since the end of February. Five more died after an attack on the Honour 25 off Somalia, from which survivors were rescued on 29 September, a reminder that the danger is no longer confined to one strait. Commercial pressure keeps ships moving into harm’s way. Reuters reported daily freight rates above $1 million drawing tonnage to load inside the Gulf, even as IMF PortWatch recorded only four transits of the Strait on 18 October against a pre-war average of around 85 a day. Every one of those transits is a crew betting on probability. The stakes explain why ships keep coming. The Strait normally carries around a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil and LNG, and each laden VLCC holds roughly two million barrels. That concentration of value and hazard in a narrow waterway makes it an ideal target, and it means every successful strike carries an environmental as well as a human price. Then came the pollution. On 23 October, the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirmed that teams were containing oil leaking from a tanker offshore. Umm Al Quwain closed its beaches and coastal areas, Sharjah closed Al Hamriya beach as a precaution, and the following day Ras Al Khaimah shut all of its beaches until further notice. There is also reports of oil pollution on some of the beaches! The ministry did not name the vessel or confirm the cause. International maritime agencies have identified it as the Gem No.2, a 330-metre tanker struck in a suspected drone attack on 9 or 10 October, from which 22 Indian seafarers were rescued. A European Space Agency radar image from 21 October showed oil leaking from a tanker about 25 kilometres off Umm Al Quwain. The IMO had already taken a political position. At MEPC 84 in the spring, member states adopted resolution MEPC.406(84), strongly condemning Iran’s attacks on merchant vessels in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz region. Condemnation, however, does not seal a ruptured cargo tank, and the engineering consequences now landing on UAE beaches demand an engineering response. It is worth asking what the international safety framework was built to do. SOLAS fire protection, detection and extinction requirements were developed largely around accidental fires: a leaking fuel pipe on a hot exhaust, an electrical fault, a cargo fire. The design assumption is an internal event, detected early, contained by structural boundaries and fought with intact systems. An external strike breaks every link in that chain at once. A missile or drone can breach structural fire boundaries, rupture fuel and cargo lines, sever cable runs and damage fire mains in a single instant. Fixed systems may be compromised before anyone reaches a release station, and the compartment designed to contain the fire may now have a hole in it. Electrical power is often the decisive weakness. Emergency generators, switchboards and their cabling are deliberately separated from main machinery spaces, but separation designed against an engine room fire may not survive blast and fragments. Loss of power means loss of fire pumps, ventilation control, steering and lighting at precisely the moment every one of them is needed. Fuel isolation is another vulnerability. Quick-closing valves and remote shutdowns work only if their air, hydraulic or electrical controls survive the initial damage. On a tanker, holed cargo tanks can add flooding, progressive leakage and stability concerns to the fire, forcing a crew trained to handle one emergency at a time to manage three simultaneously. The ISM Code requires companies to identify potential shipboard emergencies and to establish procedures, drills and exercises to respond to them. In principle, that obligation already covers attack damage. In practice, many safety management systems still treat fire, flooding and blackout as separate scenarios with separate checklists, rarely rehearsed together. The ISPS Code, adopted in the aftermath of the September 2001 attacks, was built largely around preventing unauthorised access, stowaways and terrorism through security assessments, access control and security levels. It was never intended to tell a chief engineer how to restore power after a projectile has passed through the funnel casing. That leaves a gap between security planning and damage control. Navies spend generations learning to fight fire, flooding and structural damage together, with zoned systems, redundancy and crews drilled to the point of instinct. Merchant ships carry a fraction of the crew, no dedicated damage control parties and equipment sized for accidents, and nobody should pretend otherwise. Nor is turning tankers into warships the answer. The cost would be prohibitive and the principle wrong, because the protection of merchant shipping is ultimately the responsibility of states. However, there is a substantial middle ground between doing nothing and armour plating, and much of it lies within the gift of owners, managers and their technical departments. Combined-casualty drills are the obvious starting point. Crews should rehearse a scenario in which fire, flooding and loss of main power occur together, with key personnel deemed injured and a primary control position deemed lost. Such drills are uncomfortable and often exposing, which is exactly why they are so valuable. Engineering reviews should follow. Technical departments can examine the routing of emergency power cables, the location and protection of emergency fire pumps, the independence of local controls for quick-closing valves, and whether portable pumps, smoke extraction and hull patching materials are carried in quantities sized for damage rather than routine leaks. Pollution response must sit within the same plan. A crew fighting to save a ship should know which tanks can be isolated, how cargo can be transferred within the hull, and how quickly salvage and pollution response can realistically arrive in a war zone where tugs and response vessels may themselves be targets. Gas carriers, chemical tankers and ships carrying dangerous goods deserve particular attention. A breached LPG or chemical cargo presents hazards to the crew and to surrounding coastlines that a crude spill does not, and emergency plans written for collision or grounding may not reflect the speed and violence with which an attack can escalate. Crew welfare is part of resilience too. Seafarers working under the constant threat of attack carry fatigue and stress that degrade decision-making precisely when clear thinking matters most. Rest management, honest briefings and genuine freedom to refuse unsafe passages are not soft extras; they are conditions for a crew able to fight for its ship. Abandonment presents its own dilemma. Lifeboats and liferafts are designed for a ship that is sinking or burning, not one that may be struck again while crews are mustering. Masters need clear company guidance on when to abandon, when to shelter in a protected space, and how to communicate their position when satellite positioning itself may be unreliable. Regulators have a role as well. Flag states and classification societies could usefully share anonymised damage data from this conflict, showing which systems survived, which failed and why. The industry learned hard lessons during the tanker war of the 1980s, much of that knowledge has faded, and it should not have to be relearned at the cost of further lives. The SOLAS, ISM and ISPS framework remains sound for the world it was designed for, and most ships will never face a missile. But the ships in the Gulf this autumn are facing exactly that, and their crews deserve emergency arrangements tested against the threat in front of them rather than the one imagined when the rules were written. Ships were built to survive the sea. This year has shown that some must now be prepared to survive the people on it, and the time to plan for that is before the next alarm sounds, not after. Join the leading maritime news network Incat Tasmania-built China Zorrilla, the world’s largest battery-electric ship, makes its maiden commercial crossing between Buenos Aires, Argentina, and Colonia, Uruguay. Photo: Incat Tasmania The world’s largest battery-electric ship has officially entered commercial service, marking a major milestone for the maritime industry and the growing use of electric propulsion in large passenger vessels. The 130-meter China Zorrilla , built by Australian shipbuilder Incat Tasmania for ferry operator Buquebus, completed its first commercial crossing between Buenos Aires, Argentina, and Colonia, Uruguay, on October 22. The high-speed catamaran can carry up to 2,100 passengers and 225 vehicles across the River Plate, operating entirely on battery power without the need for conventional marine engines. At the heart of the vessel is an energy storage system exceeding 40 megawatt-hours, made up of more than 250 tonnes of batteries. The system powers eight electrically driven waterjets, making China Zorrilla the largest battery-electric vessel ever constructed. The ship is supported by dedicated high-power charging infrastructure at terminals on both sides of the river, allowing its batteries to be recharged between crossings. The start of commercial service follows an official ceremony in Buenos Aires on October 21, attended by Incat Managing Director Craig Clifford, Buquebus representatives, and maritime authorities and government officials from Argentina and Uruguay. Incat Chairman Robert Clifford described the achievement as one of the proudest moments in the company’s history, and credited hundreds of workers at Incat’s Hobart shipyard with overcoming significant engineering challenges to deliver the vessel, which represents one of the most ambitious projects in the company’s history. “This ship proves that large, high-capacity commercial vessels can operate on electric power,” Clifford said. Beyond its size and technical capabilities, China Zorrilla also offers a different passenger experience. Without conventional diesel engines, the vessel operates with significantly less machinery noise and vibration, while producing no direct exhaust emissions during crossings. Craig Clifford, who traveled aboard the vessel during its maiden commercial voyage, said the difference was immediately noticeable. He noted that passengers aboard a vessel of this size would normally expect to hear and feel powerful engines operating beneath them, but that familiar noise and vibration are largely absent. The ferry also features extensive passenger amenities, including approximately 2,300 square meters of duty-free retail space. The project’s completion is particularly significant given its evolution during construction. Originally designed to use dual-fuel engines capable of burning diesel and liquefied natural gas, the vessel was ultimately redesigned for fully electric propulsion, requiring substantial engineering changes. Its entry into service demonstrates the growing potential for battery-electric technology in high-capacity ferry operations, particularly on fixed routes where shore-based charging infrastructure can support regular crossings. For Incat, the milestone is also part of a broader shift toward electric vessel construction. The Tasmanian shipbuilder is currently building three 129-meter battery-electric ferries for Danish operator Molslinjen, along with two 78-meter hybrid-electric vessels at its Hobart facility. With China Zorrilla now carrying paying passengers, the company has moved one of the maritime industry’s most ambitious electric vessel projects from the shipyard into everyday commercial operation. REUTERS/Stringer Two new maritime security warnings issued Monday point to continued dangers for commercial shipping in the Middle East, with one tanker confirmed disabled by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and another vessel reportedly on fire in the northern Persian Gulf. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it received a verified, time-late report of a tanker struck by an unknown projectile while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz on October 23 at 0839 UTC. The impact disabled the vessel, although all crew members were reported safe. UKMTO did not identify the tanker or provide details about the extent of the damage. No assessment of possible environmental impacts was available. The incident was disclosed three days after it occurred, highlighting the continuing delays in reporting attacks against commercial vessels in the region. In a separate warning issued Monday , UKMTO said it had received multiple third-party reports of a vessel on fire approximately 63 nautical miles southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq, in the northern Persian Gulf. The vessel’s identity, crew status, extent of damage and potential environmental impact were unknown. UKMTO classified the report as suspicious activity rather than a confirmed attack. The cause of the fire remains unclear, and authorities are investigating. The two reports come amid continued attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, with violence increasingly extending into the wider Persian Gulf. In its latest advisory, issued October 25 , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) maintained its SEVERE threat assessment for the Strait of Hormuz, warning that further deliberate attacks were highly likely. The assessment also kept the threat level across the wider Persian Gulf at SUBSTANTIAL , citing five attacks inside the Gulf since October 7, including incidents near anchorages and ship-to-ship transfer areas. JMIC reported 156 confirmed maritime security incidents across the region since March 1. That figure was published before UKMTO disclosed the latest verified tanker attack. The advisory highlighted another recent incident involving an LPG tanker struck by an unidentified projectile on October 22, approximately seven nautical miles northeast of Limah, Oman. That vessel subsequently reached an anchorage off Khor Fakkan. According to JMIC, Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps activity continues to include attacks, attempted attacks, drone overflights, surveillance and radio communications directing commercial vessels toward Iranian-controlled routes. The latest incidents also underscore the growing risks beyond the Strait itself, particularly in the Persian Gulf, where ships waiting at anchor or conducting cargo transfers remain exposed. Despite efforts by the United States to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, commercial traffic remains well below historical levels. JMIC reported 101 U.S.-facilitated vessel transits between October 22 and 24, compared with a historical average of approximately 138 vessels per day in 2025. The figures use different reporting methodologies, with the U.S. tally covering assisted transits rather than all commercial movements. Separate tracking data showed only single-digit daily transits outside the U.S.-facilitated system. Congestion also remains severe. As of October 25, JMIC estimated approximately 492 vessels were waiting outside the Strait of Hormuz, with large concentrations near Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and other regional anchorages. The continuing disruption comes as U.S. forces enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ports while attempting to maintain safe passage for other commercial shipping. JMIC warned that vessels using the Strait face persistent threats from projectile attacks, possible renewed mining activity and electronic navigation interference. UKMTO has advised vessels operating in the affected areas to exercise caution and report suspicious activity while investigations continue. articles.summary: Commodity trader Mercuria Energy Group accused the Baltic Exchange of continuing to publish the world’s benchmark oil tanker rate, despite distortions caused by the Iran war, because it feared losing business to a competitor.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Russia's shadow fleet vessels wait in the unofficial anchorage area in the Gulf of Finland near Vaindloo, Estonia April 10, 2026. REUTERS/Ints Kalnins (Bloomberg) — Commodity trader Mercuria Energy Group accused the Baltic Exchange of continuing to publish the world’s benchmark oil tanker rate, despite distortions caused by the Iran war, because it feared losing business to a competitor. Lawyers for Mercuria kicked off a London trial claiming that the Baltic Exchange should have suspended the benchmark rate after exports through the Strait of Hormuz were strangled by the conflict between the US, Israel and Iran. The Baltic Exchange said the commodity trader’s claim reflects “instability and opportunism.” Founded in 1774, the Baltic Exchange plays a central role in setting global shipping rates. It maintains it was still possible to put a price on the freight risk, and that it had consulted consistently with the market after the Iran war severely disrupted oil shipments through Hormuz. Flows have since recovered close to pre-war levels. In an April 14 call, a senior freight assessor described the risk of the benchmark being replaced by a competitor as “the overriding fear of what we do here,” according to a document given to the court by Mercuria’s lawyers before the hearing on Monday. Mercuria also gave examples of tanker market participants, including the Baltic Exchange’s own staff, who called into question the continued publication of a rate for the route. The trading house said that the Baltic Exchange’s freight assessor didn’t submit a value into the company’s internal system that’s supposed to represent his personal view of where the index will be. When he did eventually submit a value, it included comments such as “doesn’t make any sense to shed an opinion on this route — crazy that we have to!” The case calls into question a pricing tool that until the Iran war acted as the benchmark for oil tanker earnings across the globe. The key TD3C rate underpins contracts between tanker owners and their customers as well as billions of dollars in derivatives. It’s based on the cost of hiring a supertanker from Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura, inside the Persian Gulf, to China, and also serves as a reference point for other routes. The Baltic Exchange is confident that it has met all its statutory, contractual and regulatory obligations in the production of the TD3C benchmark, Chief Executive Officer Mark Jackson said in a statement. The claim from Mercuria is “without merit,” he added. Mercuria has “huge index-linked exposures, which it has failed to risk manage,” lawyers for the Baltic Exchange said. After being caught out by the sharp rises in the benchmark, Mercuria “wishes to unseat TD3C, and it is reaching for any available argument to do so,” they added. Mercuria’s lawyers said the evidence showed the Baltic Exchange did not suspend the index because it wanted to keep the market for certain freight agreements active, and to avoid the risk of being replaced by a rival. One of the brokers who contribute to the index said on April 2 that it was “utter nonsense” to provide an assessment of the TD3C benchmark, given the unprecedented levels of disruption to traffic through Hormuz, according to another transcript presented by Mercuria. Mercuria is urging the court to declare that the Baltic Exchange breached its obligations and ought to have suspended the TD3C route. Lawyers for the Baltic Exchange said the risk of being replaced by a rival provider did not drive its decision making. The lawyers said passage through Hormuz was still possible. “The Baltic’s decision to continue publishing TD3C, was a decision which was not taken lightly,” lawyers for exchange said in a court document countering Mercuria’s allegations. The Iran war threw global commodity markets into turmoil by slashing shipments through Hormuz, which Tehran declared closed in the early days of the conflict. In recent months, volumes have recovered, with most trackers seeing shipments close to pre-war levels. A spokesperson for Mercuria didn’t immediately respond to an email for comment. Mercuria initially said it had incurred losses estimated to be in the hundreds of millions of US dollars as a result of the Baltic Exchange continuing to publish the index, but removed any estimate of financial losses from its most recent claim. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Singapore Yards Chase Profit From Europe’s Offshore Wind Push
articles.summary: At a shipyard in northern Singapore, a yellow platform towers over a maze of scaffolding and cranes. Resembling a 15-story building, the piece will be shipped halfway around the world to Europe to be installed into an offshore wind farm.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy U.S. Department of Energy (Bloomberg) — At a shipyard in northern Singapore, a yellow platform towers over a maze of scaffolding and cranes. Resembling a 15-story building, the piece will be shipped halfway around the world to Europe to be installed into an offshore wind farm. The 30,000-ton platform, known as a high-voltage direct current converter, is scheduled to leave Seatrium Ltd.’s yard for the North Sea in 2028, where it will sit 60 kilometers offshore and help transmit electricity generated by wind turbines back to land. It’s the latest effort by Singapore to tap into Europe’s green push. Singapore is repurposing expertise built over decades serving the largest offshore oil and gas companies for the energy transition. One of the biggest opportunities is exporting these enormous converters — known as HVDC platforms — to Europe, where the technology is widely used to transmit offshore wind power over long distances. The specialized technology is one bright spot in an otherwise battered offshore wind industry. Investment plummeted 72% year-on-year globally to about $12 billion in the first half of 2026, according to BloombergNEF. Yet few yards have the expertise and capacity to build the platforms, threatening a supply bottleneck as the European Union pushes ahead with plans to expand capacity. Seatrium’s platforms, each designed to handle about 2 gigawatts of electricity, are the largest of their kind in the world. It takes five years to construct one platform, which will operate for 40 years. GE Vernova Inc. supplies the HVDC technology in the platforms. The city-state and nearby islands now account for up to 20% of global capacity outside of China for the platforms, according to Ember analyst Lam Pham, up from a negligible share just a few years ago. Demand is poised to rise as Europe builds wind farms further out to sea, giving the region’s shipyards an opportunity to capture more of the business. “The country has invested, the company has invested — and this is a showcase of what is possible,” said Chris Ong, chief executive officer of Seatrium. Seatrium, which is partly owned by Singapore state investor Temasek Holdings Pte, was tapped by European grid operator TenneT Holding BV to build four platforms for North Sea clusters. About 7,000 workers will build the structures at yards in Singapore and Batam, an Indonesian island that’s 50 minutes away by ferry. Each platform, along with connecting infrastructure, costs as much as €5 billion ($5.6 billion) each, according to TenneT. Such platforms will be critical to unlocking growth in the global offshore wind industry, which faces challenges including high costs, supply chain shortages and regulatory hurdles. Despite these hurdles, Europe is still pressing ahead with a massive expansion of offshore wind to meet ambitious green energy goals. The UK awarded a record 8.2 gigawatts of capacity in its latest subsidy auction, while Germany and the Netherlands are implementing new revenue-protection mechanisms. With enough state support, BNEF expects installations to double by the end of the decade, led by China, UK and Germany. Singapore is now trying to position itself as the top choice for European developers. Rival yards in the Middle East are upended by the regional conflict; China and South Korea are mostly meeting domestic demand; and Europe’s shipyards are being taken up for building defence-related vessels. “Singapore would make it cheaper, even including the higher shipping costs, because the industry is very labor-intensive and labor costs in Europe are super high,” said Ember’s Lam. While wind turbines generate alternating current electricity, offshore developers use HVDC platforms to convert that power to direct current, allowing it to travel longer distances with less energy loss along the way. This will become a growing trend as wind farms move further from crowded shores. Ong – who was CEO of oil rig-builder Keppel Offshore & Marine before it was merged with Sembcorp Marine to form Seatrium in 2023 – is hoping to capitalize on offshore wind demand over the next two years. The company was chasing S$9 billion ($7 billion) worth of HVDC and HVAC projects across Europe and Asia Pacific as of July. Clean energy-related contracts currently make up about 40% of the company’s order book. In the yard in Singapore, the future of offshore wind power is slowly taking shape, with welders hunched over steel panels, piecing together the massive yellow structure one module at a time. For Ong, the demand for this infrastructure is not only being driven by the energy transition — it is part of Europe’s effort to secure future power supply. “The scale and the massive need for offshore wind is a big security drive,” he said. “It has to happen.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. October 26, 2026 © Saildrone © Saildrone Saildrone announced a year-long mission with the Swedish Armed Forces to deliver persistent maritime domain awareness across Sweden’s territorial waters and exclusive economic zone in the Baltic Sea. Under the agreement, Saildrone will deploy and operate four Voyager unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) for 360 days each, representing 1,440 contracted vehicle-days of continuous maritime security operations. This deployment marks the first national deployment of Saildrone USVs under the Nordic Defence Cooperation (NORDEFCO) framework that enables participating Nordic nations to rapidly procure Saildrone maritime domain awareness services. Additional national deployments under the framework will follow. The 12-month commitment highlights a shift toward long-term operational capabilities, with the Swedish Armed Forces securing a full year of persistent maritime domain awareness to safeguard critical waters from the outset. NORDEFCO is a cooperative organization that unites Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, and other Northern European countries to streamline defense cooperation and field proven regional security solutions. The Saildrone Voyager fleet will continuously patrol Sweden’s territorial waters in the Baltic Sea, delivering real-time maritime intelligence directly to the Swedish Armed Forces. Operating as a managed service, Saildrone maintains, deploys, and tasks the USVs, enabling Sweden to maintain persistent maritime domain awareness without deploying additional crewed ships. Saildrone also recently registered four Saildrone Voyager USVs in Denmark to operate under the Danish national flag. The registration establishes a clear flag-state framework for Saildrone USVs operating internationally and supports the company operating alongside various European nations. Saildrone Europe will flag additional Saildrone USVs in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Middle East Officials Meet Discuss Deescalation Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks
articles.summary: Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the…
articles.body: Middle East Officials Meet Discuss Deescalation Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 © mykhailo - stock.adobe.com Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the Gulf kingdom. The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations — which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August — since a war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran also spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the visit was intended to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation". Saudi Arabia was represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said. Iranian state media published pictures of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, attending the meeting. Pakistan and Qatar have led mediation efforts in the war. Qatari mediators were in Tehranon Sunday, an official told Reuters. Earlier efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June but fighting between Iran and the United States soon resumed. Conflict then flared between the Iran-aligned Houthis and US ally Saudi Arabia, opening a new front. US AND IRAN THREATEN NEW ATTACKS The wider fighting has restricted shipping through the energy chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz, pushed up global oil and gas prices, left Gulf states facing missile and drone attacks, and caused a new humanitarian crisis in Yemen. Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran. Iranian security officials have told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again. The war, which earlier in the year also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese Hezbollah militia, has eroded Trump's approval ratings ahead of the midterm elections that decide control of Congress. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday's discussions would include "Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and the repercussions of US and Israeli military action against Iran". Baghaei said the meeting, proposed when Munir visited Tehran last week, could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms. A senior Pakistani security official said the focus of Monday's meeting was to build a regional non-aggression network. The agenda also included US-Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports, the official said. An Iranian official said there would be no discussion of Iran's nuclear programme at Monday's meeting and the issue would not be addressed until Tehran's demands for ending the war were met. Those conditions include ending a US blockade of Iranian ports and lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports. US Vice President JD Vance has said Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war. Pakistan's military media office and Turkey's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. PARLIAMENT APPROVES EGYPTIAN DEFENCE SUPPORT FOR SAUDIS Saudi Arabia has ⁠intensified strikes against the Houthis since they captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing against Saudi-backed government forces. The Houthis have hit Saudi airports, ports and oil installations. On Monday, the Houthis said they had ‌attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as well as Riyadh airport, which said it had resumed operations at two terminals a day earlier. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks. The parliament in Egypt, which is not a signatory to the Mecca pact, on Monday authorised the Egyptian military to help defend Saudi Arabia, a major financial and political partner for Cairo. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement says signatories shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters. The pact's members held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week. (Reuters)

articles.body: Oil Prices Fall Amidst Hopes of Easing US-Iran Hostilities Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 © Adobe Stock/chakisatelier Oil prices fell $2 a barrel on Monday amid hopes of easing hostilities between the United States and Iran, but persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia kept investors wary and prices near six-month highs. Brent crude futures were down $2.03, or 1.7%, at $114.70 at 10:37 a.m. ET (1437 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $2.60, or 2.5%, at $100.71 per barrel. On Friday, prices settled more than $3 higher, with Brent finishing the week up 6% and WTI ending the week 2.3% higher. "With the jeopardy doubled by Houthi attacks into Saudi, any Brent price dips back to the lows of last week will find grateful buyers," PVM Oil Associates analyst John Evans said. "Corrective processes are notoriously difficult to quantify, but this one has nowhere near reached any sort of levels where bulls might abandon hope," he said. Saudi Arabia, which along with Turkey and Pakistan was set to hold talks with Iranian officials in Tehran, said it was important to open channels for negotiations. IRAN WAR MEDIATION EFFORTS RESUME On Sunday, Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran to try to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation said. Despite the mediation talks, attacks continued over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had struck pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pipeline and Riyadh airport. Saudi Arabia said on Sunday it had intercepted more missiles and drones. The effects of the US-Israeli war with Iran that began on February 28 continue to reverberate as companies adjust to the disruptions of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait caused by the conflict. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. An oil spill from a strike-damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns. Elsewhere, Russian refiners are raising diesel production in October after the government granted export quotas following the Kremlin's supply agreement with the United States, two industry people close to the matter said. Energy ministers from Saudi Arabia and Singapore said state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco would start storing crude oil in Singapore from the second half of 2027, to make Aramco's supply chain in the region more resilient. The head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, reiterated supply concerns, saying on Monday at an industry event in Singapore that he did not expect energy markets in 2027 to return to where they were before the Iran war. (Reuters)

articles.title: How Trump’s Energy Dominance Turned Into Hubris
articles.summary: When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, “energy dominance” was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections.

REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo By Ron Bousso LONDON, Oct 24 (Reuters) – When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, “energy dominance” was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections. Ironically, it was the US position as the world’s top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career. In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance. Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices. What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris. UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country’s onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets. US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system. Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine. On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to “unleash American energy”, prioritizing oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables. Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”. ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy. The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region. In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the Arctic territory. The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after Washington removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation. The US subsequently took control of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test. THE IRAN QUAGMIRE The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief. Those assumptions have not aged well. The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption. This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude LCOc1 peaking at $118 a barrel in March. That was well below the record $145 reached in 2008, when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock. Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110. The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington’s Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unraveled longstanding supply routes and sent shipping prices skyrocketing. Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind. PAIN AT THE PUMP In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market. Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year. But that protection has been far from ironclad. US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while diesel surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed. Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3. The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including easing biofuel blending mandates and, most controversially, reaching a diesel supply agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices. Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households. While Trump briefly floated the idea of a diesel export ban, officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics. ‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’ The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centers underpinning the artificial intelligence race. But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security. For countries dependent on imports, particularly many in Asia, the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity. That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years. Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had balked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas. But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home. Hubris can be a dangerous thing. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Horizon Maritime The Louisiana-based Chouest Group has acquired Canadian marine and offshore services provider Horizon Maritime, expanding its presence across Canada’s East and West coasts and into the Arctic. The deal, announced Monday, brings together Chouest’s global offshore support fleet, subsea capabilities, shipbuilding operations and marine technology businesses with Horizon Maritime’s established Canadian operations and expertise in harsh-environment offshore services. Horizon Maritime, based in St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador, was acquired from CFFI and its lender, HPS, through a strategic partnership with the company’s founders. Financial terms were not disclosed. The acquisition gives Chouest a stronger foothold in Canada’s offshore energy, Arctic and marine sectors, while providing Horizon access to a much larger fleet and range of specialized services. “We are excited to welcome Horizon Maritime to the Chouest Group,” said Dino Chouest. “We see immense value in Horizon’s team, leadership and operational excellence.” “Combining Chouest’s global fleet expertise and technology with Horizon’s local footprint across Canada’s vast coastlines opens up incredible growth potential across Canada’s East Coast, West Coast and Arctic regions,” he added. Horizon Maritime specializes in marine operations in challenging environments, with experience supporting offshore energy projects, Arctic operations and other specialized maritime activities. The company has also developed relationships with Indigenous communities and organizations across Canada. Under the agreement, Horizon will retain its existing management team and leadership structure. Steve Widmeyer will continue as CEO, while Widmeyer and co-founder Sean Leet will join the company’s board of directors. The companies said the arrangement will ensure continuity for existing customers, ongoing projects and crewing operations while opening the door to expanded services across the country. For Horizon, the deal also comes as Canada looks to strengthen its maritime capabilities, particularly in the Arctic, where commercial activity, infrastructure development and national security interests are increasingly overlapping. “This is an opportunity to build on what we have created and take Horizon Maritime into its next phase of growth,” said Leet. “The Chouest Group brings significant marine experience, assets and capabilities that will help us scale Horizon Maritime’s offerings to provide increased services and support to our valued customers, while increasing dual-use capacity at a key moment in time for our region and our country.” Widmeyer emphasized the opportunities the partnership creates for Horizon’s employees, including career development and long-term growth. The companies also said they remain committed to expanding Indigenous participation in Canada’s marine economy. The acquisition extends the reach of the privately held, family-owned Chouest Group, which operates across offshore vessel ownership and operations, shipbuilding, subsea services, specialized engineering and advanced technology manufacturing. For Horizon Maritime, the combination provides access to Chouest’s global resources while maintaining its Canadian management and established customer relationships. REUTERS/Loren Elliott A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers is warning major banks and port authorities against facilitating Russian diesel shipments under President Donald Trump’s controversial agreement with Vladimir Putin, raising the prospect of legal action and congressional investigations as tankers carrying Russian fuel begin heading toward American ports. In an October 24 letter , lawmakers called on six major financial institutions and port authorities in Texas and New York to preserve records related to Russian diesel transactions, including shipping documents, vessel records, contracts and communications with government officials. The letter, first reported by Axios , warns that importing Russian diesel into the United States raises serious legal questions and could expose companies involved in the trade to future investigations. The warning was sent to JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, as well as port authorities overseeing Houston, Beaumont, Corpus Christi and the Port of New York and New Jersey. Lawmakers urged the institutions not to participate in the purchase, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing or distribution of Russian-origin diesel in the United States. They also called on the companies to avoid facilitating shipments to other international markets under the administration’s temporary sanctions relief. The effort was led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and signed by Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), along with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.). Several of the Democratic signatories could lead powerful congressional committees if their party wins control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. The lawmakers requested confirmation by October 28 that relevant records are being preserved, including shipping documents, contracts and communications related to Russian diesel transactions. The warning comes as the first Russian diesel shipments approach the United States following Trump’s October 9 agreement with Moscow, which temporarily eased sanctions in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices. As gCaptain reported, the Vietnamese-flagged tanker PVT Azura (IMO 9423683), carrying approximately 109,000 barrels of Russian diesel, is signaling Norfolk, Virginia, as its destination, with an expected arrival on November 2. Another tanker, the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes, loaded approximately 40,000 metric tons of diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22. Reuters reported the vessel was signaling New York, with an estimated arrival on November 7. Neither shipment has been confirmed as destined for a U.S. buyer. Under the agreement, Russia committed to supplying an initial 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter. The Treasury Department subsequently issued General License 135, authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. But lawmakers argue the arrangement conflicts with the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibited imports of Russian petroleum products following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. They contend that the administration cannot simply waive those statutory restrictions. The Treasury Department maintains that the agreement is legal, while the White House has defended the move as necessary to ease energy costs amid severe market disruptions caused by the war with Iran. For the maritime industry, the dispute adds uncertainty to a trade Washington has just moved to reopen. Shipowners, charterers, insurers, banks and terminal operators now face the prospect of facilitating shipments that lawmakers are already threatening to investigate. articles.title: Eni gets the ball rolling on execution of Mediterranean gas project
articles.summary: Eni has kicked off the execution phase of Cyprus's 3 trillion cubic feet (tcf) gas project, targeting first production by H1 2028.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects October 26, 2026 · 21 hours ago Eni gets the ball rolling on execution of Mediterranean gas project Eni has kicked off the execution phase of Cyprus's 3 trillion cubic feet (tcf) gas project, targeting first production by H1 2028. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Map of the Cronos natural gas field development project in Block 6 offshore of Cyprus Source: TotalEnergies Italy’s energy giant Eni has fired the starting gun on the execution chapter of its Eastern Mediterranean project, awarding construction and drilling contracts to fast-track Cyprus's first-ever commercial gas development, which is expected to reach production of up to 500 million standard cubic feet per day (scf/d) in the first half of 2028, with gas to be processed and liquefied in Egypt before being shipped primarily to European markets. Eni has signed the main engineering, procurement, construction (EPC) and drilling contracts for the development of the Cronos project, marking the start of the project's execution phase and a key milestone towards the monetization of Cyprus' first gas development. According to the Italian giant, these contracts include floating control unit, transportation and installations, offshore seal lines, subsea production system, flexible lines, umbilicals, onshore line EPC, and drilling rig services. The contracting activity follows the final investment decision (FID) reached on July 28, 2026, for the development of the Cronos gas discovery in Block 6 offshore Cyprus. Related Articles Fossil Energy Cronos nexus unbound: Egypt and Cyprus put pen to paper for gas field development 3 min read With resources estimated at more than 3 tcf of gas initially in place, the project is expected to reach a production plateau of up to 500 million standard cubic feet per day, with start-up expected in H1 2028. The development will leverage a fast-track approach based on regional integration and the use of existing infrastructure. The execution phase was formally launched in Nicosia during a ceremony attended by Nikos Christodoulides , President of the Republic of Cyprus; Michael Damianos , Minister of Energy, Commerce, and Industry of the Republic of Cyprus; and Guido Brusco , Eni’s Chief Operating Officer of Global Natural Resources. Related Articles Fossil Energy Eni and TotalEnergies take FID for Cyprus’ first gas development 2 min read Gas produced from Cronos will be transported to Egypt, where it will be processed through existing facilities, including the Zohr infrastructure , before being liquefied at the Damietta LNG plant for export to international markets, primarily Europe. Block 6 is operated by Eni with a 50% interest, alongside its partner, TotalEnergies, which holds the remaining half. The Italian firm also operates Block 8 in Cyprus and holds participating interests in Blocks 7 and 11, which are operated by TotalEnergies. Eni highlighted: “As Eni's first development project in Cyprus and the country's first hydrocarbon development, Cronos represents a strategic milestone for the Republic of Cyprus. “The project will support the country's emergence as a natural gas producer and exporter while strengthening the integration of energy systems across the Eastern Mediterranean using existing Egyptian gas and LNG infrastructure.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go!
